HT-01.Front desk: The department that checks guests in and out, issues keys and answers questions. Also called the front office, it is the guest's main point of contact.
HT-01.Housekeeping: The department that cleans guest rooms and public areas and supplies fresh linens and towels. It is often the largest department by staff count.
HT-01.Food and beverage: Runs the hotel's restaurants, bars, kitchens and room service. Often shortened to F&B, it is usually the second biggest source of revenue after rooms.
HT-01.Management: The executive office, led by the general manager, that sets goals and oversees every other department in the hotel.
HT-01.Concierge: A guest-service desk that books restaurants, tickets and tours and gives local advice, helping guests with requests beyond the room itself.
HT-01.Sales and marketing: The team that promotes the hotel and sells rooms and meeting space, especially to groups, companies and event planners.
HT-01.Reservations: Takes and manages room bookings made by phone, online or through travel agents, and keeps track of how many rooms are left to sell.
HT-01.Maintenance: Also called engineering, this department repairs equipment and keeps the building's heating, plumbing, lighting and grounds working.
HT-01.Human resources: Recruits, hires and trains employees and handles pay, benefits and workplace rules for the whole hotel.
HT-01.Accounting: Records the hotel's income and expenses, pays bills and staff, and prepares financial reports. It is headed by the controller.
HT-01.Security: Protects guests, staff and property by patrolling, watching cameras and responding to emergencies. Some hotels call it loss prevention.
HT-01.Banquets: The department that sets up and serves food at weddings, meetings and other functions held in the hotel's event rooms.
HT-01.Valet: Part of uniformed services, the staff who park guests' cars, carry luggage and open doors at the hotel entrance.
HT-01.Spa and recreation: Operates the spa, pool, fitness center and leisure activities, which earn extra revenue and attract guests to resorts.
HT-01.Rooms division: The large division that groups together the front office, housekeeping, reservations and uniformed services, all the areas that deliver the guest room.
HT-01.Revenue management: A specialist team that adjusts room rates and availability day by day to match demand, aiming to earn the most from a fixed number of rooms.
HT-01.Purchasing: Buys the food, linens, supplies and equipment the hotel needs, comparing suppliers to get the right quality at the best price.
HT-01.Information technology: Looks after the hotel's computers, booking systems, Wi-Fi, phones and key-card systems. Usually shortened to IT.
HT-01.Retail: Runs the gift shop or lobby store that sells snacks, toiletries, souvenirs and clothing to guests.

HT-02.Hotel: A building that rents rooms to travelers by the night, usually with services such as a front desk and daily housekeeping.
HT-02.Motel: Short for motor hotel. A low-rise roadside property where room doors usually open onto the parking lot, built for travelers arriving by car.
HT-02.Resort: A property that guests visit as a destination in itself, with recreation such as pools, beaches, golf or skiing on site.
HT-02.Bed and breakfast: A small, often owner-run property, usually a converted house, where the room price includes a morning meal.
HT-02.Hostel: Low-cost lodging where guests rent a bed in a shared dormitory room and share kitchens and bathrooms. Popular with young and budget travelers.
HT-02.Vacation rental: A privately owned house, apartment or villa rented to travelers for short stays, often booked through sites such as Airbnb or Vrbo.
HT-02.Inn: A small lodging property, often in a rural area or a historic building, with a personal feel and usually a place to eat.
HT-02.Luxury hotel: A top-tier hotel with high prices, large well-furnished rooms and very personal service, such as a five-star property.
HT-02.Budget hotel: A limited-service hotel that keeps prices low by offering a clean basic room with few extras such as restaurants or room service.
HT-02.Campground: An outdoor site where travelers pay to pitch a tent or park a recreational vehicle, often with shared restrooms and hookups.
HT-02.Lodge: A property in a natural setting, such as near a ski slope or national park, built for guests who come for outdoor activities.
HT-02.Boutique hotel: A small, stylish hotel with its own distinct design and personality, in contrast to the standard look of a large chain.
HT-02.Cabin: A small, simple house, usually wooden and in the woods or mountains, rented as a private stand-alone unit.
HT-02.Condominium: A privately owned apartment-style unit with a kitchen and living area that the owner rents to travelers when not using it.
HT-02.Full-service hotel: A hotel offering a wide range of services on site, including a restaurant, room service, meeting space and bell staff.
HT-02.Guest house: A private home turned into a small, simple lodging business, offering a few rooms at modest prices. Called a pension in parts of Europe.
HT-02.Extended stay: A hotel designed for stays of a week or more, with a kitchen in each room and lower rates for longer bookings.
HT-02.Timeshare: Vacation ownership in which buyers purchase the right to use a unit for a set period each year, sharing the property with other owners.
HT-02.Glamping: Short for glamorous camping. Outdoor stays in furnished tents, yurts or domes with real beds and other comforts.
HT-02.Casino hotel: A hotel attached to a gambling floor. Rooms may be priced low or given free because gaming brings in most of the revenue.
HT-02.All-suite hotel: A hotel in which every unit is a suite, with a living area separate from the sleeping area.
HT-02.Airport hotel: A hotel located next to an airport, serving travelers with early flights, long layovers or canceled flights, plus airline crews.
HT-02.Capsule hotel: A hotel, first popular in Japan, that rents small sleeping pods stacked side by side instead of full rooms.
HT-02.Ryokan: A traditional Japanese inn with tatami-mat floors, futon beds, shared baths and meals served to guests as part of the stay.
HT-02.Homestay: Paid lodging in a local family's home, where the guest lives alongside the hosts and experiences their daily life.
HT-02.Dude ranch: A working or former cattle ranch that hosts paying guests for horseback riding and other Western outdoor activities.
HT-02.Conference center: A property designed mainly for meetings, with purpose-built meeting rooms plus guest rooms and meals sold as one package.

HT-03.Lodging: The segment that sells overnight accommodation, including hotels, motels, resorts and vacation rentals.
HT-03.Airlines: Companies that carry passengers by air. Air travel makes long-distance and international tourism practical.
HT-03.Food and beverage: Restaurants, bars and other businesses that feed travelers. Eating out is one of the biggest things visitors spend money on.
HT-03.Cruise lines: Companies that operate passenger ships combining transportation, lodging, dining and entertainment in a single vacation.
HT-03.Transportation: The businesses that move travelers from place to place, such as railroads, bus and motorcoach companies and other ground transport.
HT-03.Attractions: Places people travel to see or experience, such as theme parks, museums, national parks and landmarks.
HT-03.Recreation: Businesses and facilities offering leisure activities such as skiing, golf, boating and hiking that travelers take part in.
HT-03.Travel agencies: Businesses, in shops or online, that book flights, hotels and tours for travelers and usually earn a commission or fee.
HT-03.Entertainment: Live shows, concerts, sports and other performances that draw visitors and give them something to do during a trip.
HT-03.Tour operators: Companies that bundle transport, lodging and sightseeing into packaged tours and sell them to travelers or through agents.
HT-03.Meetings and events: The segment that plans and hosts conventions, conferences, trade shows and incentive trips, often called MICE (meetings, incentives, conferences and exhibitions).
HT-03.Car rental: Companies that rent vehicles to travelers by the day or week, often from counters at airports.
HT-03.Business travel: Trips taken for work, such as sales calls and meetings. Business travelers often book late and pay higher prices.
HT-03.Gaming: The casino and gambling segment. Places such as Las Vegas and Macau built their tourism around it.
HT-03.Ecotourism: Responsible travel to natural areas that protects the environment and benefits the local people who live there.
HT-03.Shopping: Retail aimed at visitors, from souvenir shops to outlet malls. For some trips, shopping is a main reason to go.
HT-03.Adventure tourism: Travel built around physical, often risky outdoor activities such as rafting, climbing, trekking or zip-lining.
HT-03.Cultural tourism: Travel to experience a place's history, arts, traditions and way of life, such as visiting heritage sites and festivals.
HT-03.Destination marketing organizations: Groups, such as a convention and visitors bureau or tourism board, that promote a city or region to visitors and conventions.
HT-03.Medical tourism: Travel to another city or country to receive medical or dental care, often because it costs less or is available sooner.
HT-03.Timeshare: The vacation ownership segment, where people buy the right to use a resort unit for a set time each year.

HT-04.Swimming pool: An indoor or outdoor pool for guests to use. It is one of the features families look for most when choosing a hotel.
HT-04.Free Wi-Fi: Wireless internet access included in the room price. Most guests now expect it as a basic part of a stay.
HT-04.Free breakfast: A morning meal included in the room rate, ranging from a simple continental spread to a hot buffet.
HT-04.Fitness center: An exercise room with equipment such as treadmills and weights that guests can use during their stay.
HT-04.Parking: A place for guests to leave their cars, either self-parked or handled by a valet. It may be free or charged per night.
HT-04.Spa: A facility offering massages, facials and other relaxation treatments, usually for an extra charge.
HT-04.Restaurant or bar: A place to eat or drink inside the hotel, so guests do not have to leave the property for a meal.
HT-04.Room service: Food and drinks ordered from the hotel kitchen and delivered to the guest's room. Also called in-room dining.
HT-04.Airport shuttle: A van or bus that carries guests between the hotel and the airport, often at no charge.
HT-04.Television: An in-room TV with cable channels or streaming apps, a standard feature guests expect for entertainment.
HT-04.Hot tub or sauna: A heated whirlpool bath or a dry-heat room where guests can relax, often located beside the pool.
HT-04.Daily housekeeping: Cleaning of the room each day of the stay, including making the bed and replacing towels.
HT-04.Business center: A room with computers, printers and sometimes a copier where guests can do work while traveling.
HT-04.Toiletries: Small bathroom supplies such as soap, shampoo, conditioner and lotion that the hotel provides free in each room.
HT-04.Laundry service: Washing or dry cleaning of guests' clothes by the hotel for a fee, or coin-operated machines guests use themselves.
HT-04.Air conditioning: Cooling that guests can usually control from a thermostat in the room, important for comfort in warm climates.
HT-04.Coffee maker: A machine in the room with free coffee and tea supplies, so guests can make a hot drink without going out.
HT-04.Mini fridge: A small refrigerator in the room where guests can keep their own drinks, snacks or medicine cold.
HT-04.Meeting rooms: Spaces the hotel rents out for conferences, training sessions and banquets, often with audiovisual equipment.
HT-04.Minibar: A small in-room fridge stocked with drinks and snacks that guests pay for if they use them.
HT-04.Concierge service: Staff who arrange restaurant bookings, tickets, tours and transport and give advice about the local area.
HT-04.Pet-friendly rooms: Rooms where guests may bring a dog or cat, sometimes for an extra cleaning fee or deposit.
HT-04.Hair dryer: A small appliance supplied in the bathroom so guests do not need to pack their own.
HT-04.Iron and ironing board: Supplied in the room so guests, especially business travelers, can press wrinkled clothes.
HT-04.Bathrobes: Robes, sometimes with slippers, placed in the room for guests to wear during the stay. Common in upscale hotels and spas.
HT-04.Kitchenette: A small cooking area in the room with items such as a sink, microwave and fridge, common in extended-stay hotels.
HT-04.Golf course: A course on the property where guests can play, usually for a fee. It is a major draw for resorts.
HT-04.Gift shop: A small store in the lobby selling souvenirs, snacks and travel items guests may have forgotten.
HT-04.Vending and ice machines: Self-service machines, usually on each floor, where guests can buy snacks and drinks and fill an ice bucket for free.
HT-04.In-room safe: A small lockable box in the room, opened with a code the guest sets, for passports, cash and other valuables.
HT-04.Turndown service: An evening visit by housekeeping to fold back the bed covers, tidy the room and prepare it for sleep. Typical of luxury hotels.
HT-04.Luggage storage: A secure place where staff hold guests' bags before check-in or after check-out so they can explore without them.
HT-04.Wake-up call: A phone call to the room at a time the guest requests, made by the front desk or an automated system.
HT-04.Childcare: Supervised care for children, such as a kids' club or babysitting, that frees parents to enjoy other activities.
HT-04.Electric vehicle charging: Charging stations in the parking lot or garage where guests with electric cars can recharge overnight.
HT-04.Free newspaper: A daily paper left at the door or offered in the lobby at no charge, a traditional extra for business travelers.

HT-05.Listen: Give the guest full attention and let them explain without interrupting. Guests want to feel heard before anything else.
HT-05.Apologize: Say sorry sincerely for the guest's bad experience, even if the problem was not your fault. It shows the business cares.
HT-05.Fix the problem: Take action that corrects what went wrong, such as replacing a meal or moving the guest to another room.
HT-05.Stay calm: Keep a polite, even tone and avoid becoming defensive, even if the guest is angry. A calm employee helps cool the situation.
HT-05.Show empathy: Let the guest know you understand how they feel and why they are upset. It shows their concern is being taken seriously.
HT-05.Thank the guest: Thank them for speaking up. A complaint gives the business a chance to fix a problem that silent guests would just walk away from.
HT-05.Ask questions: Ask for the details needed to understand exactly what happened, so the solution fits the real problem.
HT-05.Involve a manager: Pass the complaint to a supervisor when it is serious or beyond what the employee is allowed to resolve.
HT-05.Offer compensation: Give something to make up for the trouble, such as a discount, refund, free meal or room upgrade.
HT-05.Take ownership: Accept responsibility for getting the problem solved instead of passing the guest to someone else or saying it is not your job.
HT-05.Act quickly: Respond right away. The longer a guest waits for a fix, the more upset they become.
HT-05.Offer options: Give the guest a choice of solutions, or ask what would make it right. Having a say helps the guest feel in control.
HT-05.Follow up: Check back with the guest afterward to make sure the solution worked and that they are now satisfied.
HT-05.Restate the complaint: Repeat the problem back in your own words to confirm you understood it correctly before trying to solve it.
HT-05.Explain what will be done: Tell the guest exactly what you will do and how long it will take, so they know what to expect.
HT-05.Follow company policy: Handle the complaint within the business's rules, such as limits on refunds, so every guest is treated fairly and consistently.
HT-05.Document the complaint: Write down what happened and how it was resolved, so managers can spot patterns and other staff know the history.
HT-05.Avoid placing blame: Do not argue, make excuses or blame the guest or a coworker. Blame does not solve the problem and makes the guest angrier.
HT-05.Speak in private: Move the conversation away from other guests when possible. It spares the guest embarrassment and keeps the scene from disturbing others.
HT-05.Prevent it from happening again: Find the root cause of the complaint and change the process or training so other guests do not face the same problem.

HT-06.Economic conditions: The overall health of the economy. In a recession people cut back on trips first, while in good times they travel more.
HT-06.Weather: Storms, heat or cold at the destination or along the route. Bad weather cancels trips, while good weather encourages them.
HT-06.Seasonality: The regular rise and fall of demand through the year, with busy peak seasons and quiet off seasons.
HT-06.Fuel prices: The cost of gasoline and jet fuel. When fuel is expensive, driving costs more and airlines raise fares, so fewer people travel.
HT-06.Holidays: Public holidays and school breaks, when many people are free at the same time and demand for travel jumps.
HT-06.Safety concerns: Fear of crime or terrorism at a destination. Travelers avoid places they believe are dangerous.
HT-06.Disease outbreaks: The spread of an illness, such as the COVID-19 pandemic, which can stop people traveling and close borders.
HT-06.Natural disasters: Events such as hurricanes, earthquakes and wildfires that damage a destination and keep visitors away, sometimes for months.
HT-06.Competition: Rival destinations and businesses. If a competing place cuts prices or opens a new attraction, travelers may go there instead.
HT-06.Airfare: The price of a plane ticket. Because it is often the biggest cost of a trip, cheaper fares bring more visitors.
HT-06.Disposable income: The money households have left after taxes. The more people have to spend, the more they can afford to travel.
HT-06.Exchange rates: The value of one currency against another. A strong home currency makes trips abroad cheaper, and a weak one makes them cost more.
HT-06.Special events: Large events such as the Olympics, festivals or concerts that draw crowds of visitors to a place for a short time.
HT-06.Trends and social media: Shifts in what is fashionable. A place that goes viral online or appears in a hit show can see a sudden rush of visitors.
HT-06.Political instability: War, protests or unrest in a country. Travelers stay away from places where the government or streets seem unsafe.
HT-06.Visa and entry rules: A country's requirements for foreign visitors. Strict or costly rules, or travel bans, reduce the number who come.
HT-06.Government regulations: Laws and taxes that affect travel, such as hotel taxes, airline rules or limits on short-term rentals.
HT-06.Technology: New tools that change how people travel. Online booking makes trips easier, while video meetings can replace some business trips.
HT-06.Leisure time: The amount of free time people have, such as paid vacation days. More time off means more chances to travel.
HT-06.Consumer confidence: How hopeful people feel about their jobs and money. When they feel secure, they are more willing to spend on trips.
HT-06.Travel advisories: Official government warnings that tell citizens how risky it is to visit a country. A strong warning cuts demand sharply.
HT-06.Demographic trends: Changes in the makeup of the population, such as more retirees with time to travel, that shift who travels and where.
HT-06.Environmental concerns: Worry about the harm travel does, such as carbon emissions from flying, which leads some people to fly less or pick greener trips.
HT-06.Transportation access: How easy it is to reach a place. A new airport, flight route or highway can open a destination to many more visitors.
HT-06.Labor strikes: Work stoppages by airline, rail or other transport staff that cancel service and disrupt or discourage travel.

HT-07.Online reviews: Ratings and comments guests post on sites such as Tripadvisor, Yelp and Google. They are public, so future customers read them too.
HT-07.Surveys: Sets of questions sent to guests by email, text or a link on the receipt, asking them to rate parts of their visit.
HT-07.Comment cards: Short printed forms left in the room or on the table for guests to write their opinions and hand in before they leave.
HT-07.Social media: Posts, comments and messages about the business on platforms such as Instagram and Facebook, which staff can monitor and answer.
HT-07.Asking guests in person: Staff or managers talk to guests during the visit, for example a manager stopping at tables, so problems can be fixed on the spot.
HT-07.Follow-up emails: Messages sent after a stay or meal thanking the guest and inviting them to share how it went.
HT-07.Mystery shoppers: People hired to pose as ordinary guests and then report in detail on the service, cleanliness and quality they experienced.
HT-07.Complaint records: A log of the problems guests report. Reviewing it shows which issues keep coming up.
HT-07.Website feedback form: A contact or feedback page on the business's own website where guests can type and send comments at any time.
HT-07.Focus groups: Small groups of guests brought together for a guided discussion about their opinions, giving detailed answers a survey cannot.
HT-07.Employee feedback: Reports from front-line staff, who hear guests' comments and complaints every day and can pass them to management.
HT-07.Follow-up phone calls: Calls made to guests after their visit to ask about the experience, often used for groups and events.
HT-07.Mobile app feedback: Ratings and comments collected through the business's own app, often right after an order or a stay.
HT-07.Customer service hotline: A phone number, often toll-free, that guests can call to report a problem or give praise.
HT-07.Observation: Watching how guests behave, such as what they leave on the plate or where lines form, to learn things they may not say.
HT-07.Feedback kiosks: Tablets or push-button stands near the exit or on the table where guests tap a quick rating before they leave.
HT-07.Live chat: Text or chat messages exchanged with guests during their stay, which reveal problems while there is still time to fix them.
HT-07.Guest advisory panel: A standing group of regular customers that a business consults from time to time about new ideas and service.

LDG-01.Single: A room sold for one person, usually with one bed.
LDG-01.Double: A room for two people, traditionally with one double (full-size) bed.
LDG-01.Suite: A larger unit with a living or sitting area separate from the bedroom, sold at a higher price than a standard room.
LDG-01.Standard room: The hotel's basic room type with the usual furnishings and the lowest regular price.
LDG-01.King: A room with one king-size bed, the largest standard bed size, popular with couples and business travelers.
LDG-01.Queen: A room with one queen-size bed, which is larger than a double but smaller than a king.
LDG-01.Twin: A room with two separate single (twin-size) beds, suited to two people who do not want to share a bed.
LDG-01.Deluxe room: A step up from a standard room, with more space, better furnishings or a better location in the hotel.
LDG-01.Family room: A larger room with enough beds for parents and children to stay together, such as a double bed plus bunk beds or a sofa bed.
LDG-01.Triple: A room set up to sleep three people, with three beds or a double bed plus a single.
LDG-01.Connecting rooms: Two rooms next to each other with a private door between them, so a family or group can move between rooms without using the hallway.
LDG-01.Quad: A room set up to sleep four people, often with two double beds.
LDG-01.Studio: A single room that combines sleeping and living space, often with a sofa bed and sometimes a small kitchen.
LDG-01.Double-double: A room with two double beds, or often two queen beds, that can sleep up to four people.
LDG-01.View room: A room sold at a higher price because it looks out on something attractive, such as the ocean, a city skyline or a garden.
LDG-01.Accessible room: A room designed for guests with disabilities, with features such as wider doors, grab bars and a roll-in shower.
LDG-01.Adjoining rooms: Rooms that are side by side and share a wall but, unlike connecting rooms, have no door between them.
LDG-01.Junior suite: One large room with a sitting area that is partly, but not fully, separated from the sleeping area.
LDG-01.Penthouse: A large luxury suite on the top floor of the hotel, usually with the best views and the highest price.
LDG-01.Executive room: A room on a special floor for business travelers, usually with a work desk and access to a private lounge.
LDG-01.Honeymoon suite: A romantic suite marketed to newlyweds, often with a king bed and extras such as a whirlpool tub.
LDG-01.Villa: A separate house or bungalow on resort grounds that gives guests more space and privacy than a room in the main building.
LDG-01.Smoking or non-smoking room: Rooms labeled by whether smoking is allowed inside. Most hotels are now mostly or entirely non-smoking.
LDG-01.Presidential suite: Usually the largest and most expensive suite in the hotel, with several rooms and the finest furnishings.
LDG-01.Hospitality suite: A suite used for entertaining rather than sleeping, where a company or group hosts guests with food and drinks.
LDG-01.Efficiency: A room that includes a small kitchen area, so guests can prepare their own meals.
LDG-01.Hollywood twin: A room with two twin beds placed together against a single shared headboard.
LDG-01.Lanai: A room with a balcony or patio that overlooks water or a garden. The word is Hawaiian for a porch.
LDG-01.Cabana: A room next to the pool area, often with direct access to it.

LDG-02.Front desk agent: The employee who checks guests in and out, issues room keys, takes payment and answers questions at the front desk.
LDG-02.Housekeeper: Also called a room attendant, the person who cleans guest rooms, makes beds and replaces towels and supplies.
LDG-02.General manager: The top manager of the hotel, responsible for its profit, its staff and the experience of every guest.
LDG-02.Bellhop: A uniformed employee who carries guests' luggage to and from their rooms and shows them the room's features.
LDG-02.Concierge: A guest-service specialist who books restaurants, tickets and tours and recommends things to do in the area.
LDG-02.Chef: A trained cook who prepares food in the hotel's kitchens. The executive chef runs the whole kitchen and plans the menus.
LDG-02.Server: The person who takes orders and brings food and drinks to guests in the hotel's restaurant or at banquets.
LDG-02.Bartender: Mixes and serves drinks at the hotel bar or lounge and checks that guests are old enough to be served alcohol.
LDG-02.Valet: Parks guests' cars when they arrive and brings them back when they are needed.
LDG-02.Doorman: Stands at the hotel entrance to greet guests, open doors, call taxis and help with luggage.
LDG-02.Night auditor: Works the overnight front desk and balances the day's accounts, checking that all room charges and payments were recorded correctly.
LDG-02.Security officer: Patrols the property, watches cameras and responds to incidents to keep guests, staff and belongings safe.
LDG-02.Reservations agent: Takes room bookings by phone or online, quotes rates and records the guest's details and requests.
LDG-02.Maintenance engineer: Repairs and maintains the building's equipment, such as plumbing, lighting, heating and air conditioning.
LDG-02.Assistant general manager: Second in command to the general manager, who helps run daily operations and takes charge when the general manager is away.
LDG-02.Room service attendant: Delivers food and drinks ordered from the kitchen to guest rooms and collects the trays afterward.
LDG-02.Shuttle driver: Drives the hotel's van or bus, carrying guests to and from the airport or nearby attractions.
LDG-02.Dishwasher: Washes dishes, pots and utensils and keeps the kitchen clean. In hotels the job is often called steward.
LDG-02.Executive housekeeper: The manager of the housekeeping department, who schedules and trains room attendants and controls cleaning supplies and linens.
LDG-02.Front office manager: Supervises the front desk staff, handles difficult guest problems and makes sure check-in and check-out run smoothly.
LDG-02.Director of sales: Leads the team that sells rooms and meeting space to groups, companies and event planners.
LDG-02.Event coordinator: Plans and oversees meetings, weddings and banquets held at the hotel, working with the client on every detail.
LDG-02.Accountant: Keeps the hotel's financial records, pays bills and prepares reports. The head of the accounting office is called the controller.
LDG-02.Human resources manager: Handles hiring, training, pay, benefits and employee relations for the hotel's staff.
LDG-02.Lifeguard: Watches swimmers at the hotel or resort pool or beach and is trained to rescue people and give first aid.
LDG-02.Spa therapist: Gives massages, facials and other treatments to guests in the hotel's spa.
LDG-02.Laundry attendant: Washes, dries, presses and folds the hotel's sheets, towels and uniforms, and sometimes guests' clothing.
LDG-02.Food and beverage director: The manager in charge of all the hotel's restaurants, bars, kitchens, banquets and room service.
LDG-02.Revenue manager: Studies demand and sets room rates and booking rules day by day so the hotel earns as much as possible from its rooms.
LDG-02.Rooms division manager: Oversees the front office, housekeeping, reservations and bell staff, the departments that deliver the guest room.
LDG-02.Switchboard operator: Answers the hotel's phone lines and connects calls. The phone system is known as the PBX, for private branch exchange.
LDG-02.Houseperson: A housekeeping worker who cleans public areas, moves heavy items and brings linens and supplies to the room attendants.
LDG-02.Groundskeeper: Looks after the hotel's lawns, gardens and outdoor areas so the property looks cared for.

LDG-03.Occupancy rate: The percentage of available rooms that were sold in a period. It equals rooms sold divided by rooms available.
LDG-03.Average daily rate: The average price paid per room sold, found by dividing room revenue by the number of rooms sold. Shortened to ADR.
LDG-03.RevPAR: Revenue per available room. Room revenue divided by all rooms available, or occupancy times average daily rate.
LDG-03.Guest satisfaction score: A rating taken from guest surveys and online reviews that shows how happy guests were with their stay.
LDG-03.Room revenue: The total money earned from selling guest rooms in a period, the main source of income for most hotels.
LDG-03.Rooms sold: The number of room nights guests paid for in a period, a basic count of how much business the hotel did.
LDG-03.Average length of stay: The average number of nights each guest stays, found by dividing room nights by the number of bookings.
LDG-03.Net promoter score: A loyalty measure based on asking guests how likely they are, from 0 to 10, to recommend the hotel to others.
LDG-03.Gross operating profit: Total revenue minus the day-to-day costs of running the hotel, before fixed charges such as rent, property taxes and insurance. It shows how well managers run the property.
LDG-03.Labor cost: The money spent on wages and benefits, often shown as a percentage of revenue. It is usually a hotel's largest expense.
LDG-03.Food and beverage revenue: Money earned from restaurants, bars, banquets and room service, an important income source beyond room sales.
LDG-03.GOPPAR: Gross operating profit per available room. It divides operating profit by rooms available, so it reflects costs as well as revenue.
LDG-03.Cost per occupied room: The average cost of servicing one sold room, covering items such as housekeeping labor, laundry and supplies.
LDG-03.Repeat guest rate: The share of guests who have stayed at the hotel before. A high rate signals loyalty and lowers marketing costs.
LDG-03.Market share: The hotel's portion of the total room business in its area, compared with competing hotels.
LDG-03.Cancellation rate: The percentage of bookings that guests cancel before arrival, which affects how many rooms a hotel can safely sell.
LDG-03.Employee turnover: The rate at which staff leave and must be replaced. High turnover raises hiring and training costs and can hurt service.
LDG-03.RevPAR index: The hotel's revenue per available room divided by the average for its competitors. A score above 100 means it is beating them.
LDG-03.Total revenue per available room: All hotel revenue, including food, spa and parking, divided by rooms available. Often written TRevPAR.
LDG-03.Market penetration index: The hotel's occupancy divided by its competitors' average occupancy. Above 100 means it is filling more than its fair share of rooms.
LDG-03.Average rate index: The hotel's average daily rate divided by its competitors' average rate, showing whether it charges more or less than they do.
LDG-03.Revenue per occupied room: Total revenue divided by the number of rooms sold, showing how much each staying guest spends in all.
LDG-03.Booking pace: The speed at which reservations for a future date are coming in, compared with the same point in earlier periods.
LDG-03.Direct booking ratio: The share of reservations made through the hotel's own website or phone line, which avoid commissions paid to outside booking sites.

LDG-04.Check-in: Registering an arriving guest: confirming the booking, collecting details and a payment method, and handing over the room.
LDG-04.Check-out: Closing a departing guest's stay by reviewing the bill, settling the account and taking back the keys.
LDG-04.Greeting guests: Welcoming each person who approaches the desk. The front desk gives most guests their first impression of the hotel.
LDG-04.Answering guest questions: Giving information about the hotel and the local area, such as directions, opening hours and places to eat.
LDG-04.Taking reservations: Booking, changing or canceling rooms for guests who call or walk up, especially when there is no separate reservations office.
LDG-04.Assigning rooms: Choosing a specific clean, vacant room that matches the room type and requests in the guest's booking.
LDG-04.Issuing room keys: Programming and handing over key cards that open only the guest's room for the nights of the stay.
LDG-04.Processing payment: Taking the guest's card or cash, authorizing the amount and settling the final bill.
LDG-04.Handling complaints: Listening to guests' problems, such as a noisy or unclean room, and fixing them or passing them to the right department.
LDG-04.Handling guest requests: Taking requests for items such as extra towels or a crib and making sure the right department delivers them.
LDG-04.Answering phones: Taking outside calls and calls from guest rooms, then answering the question or transferring the caller.
LDG-04.Verifying identification: Checking a guest's photo ID and booking at arrival to confirm the right person is being given the room.
LDG-04.Wake-up calls: Recording the time a guest asks to be woken and making sure the call is placed.
LDG-04.Posting charges: Adding room, tax, restaurant and other charges to the guest's folio, the running account of what the guest owes.
LDG-04.Upselling rooms: Offering an arriving guest a better room or added services for an extra charge, which raises the hotel's revenue.
LDG-04.Coordinating with housekeeping: Sharing room status with housekeeping so that the desk knows which rooms are clean and ready to assign.
LDG-04.Arranging transportation: Calling taxis or booking shuttles and cars for guests who need a ride.
LDG-04.Storing luggage: Tagging and holding bags for guests who arrive before their room is ready or want to explore after checking out.
LDG-04.Handling room changes: Moving a guest to a different room, for example after a complaint, and updating the keys and records.
LDG-04.Night audit: The overnight job of balancing the day's accounts, posting room charges and running the end-of-day reports.
LDG-04.Handling mail and messages: Receiving letters, packages and phone messages for guests and making sure they are delivered.
LDG-04.Currency exchange: Changing foreign money into local currency for guests, a service offered mainly by hotels with many international visitors.
LDG-04.Safe deposit boxes: Locked boxes kept at the front desk where guests can store valuables such as passports, cash and jewelry.
LDG-04.Lost and found: Logging items guests report missing or leave behind and returning them to their owners. Some hotels give this job to housekeeping.
LDG-04.Loyalty program enrollment: Signing guests up for the hotel brand's rewards program at check-in, so they earn points and are more likely to return.

LDG-05.Group rate: A discounted price for a block of rooms booked together, for example for a convention, tour or wedding party.
LDG-05.Rack rate: The full published price of a room before any discount. Most guests pay less than this rate.
LDG-05.Corporate rate: A discounted rate a hotel negotiates with a company whose employees stay often, in return for steady business.
LDG-05.Government rate: A reduced rate for government employees traveling on official business, often matched to the government's daily lodging allowance.
LDG-05.AAA rate: A discount for members of the American Automobile Association (AAA), a large auto club whose members travel often.
LDG-05.Member rate: A lower price offered only to people who have joined the hotel brand's loyalty program, to encourage sign-ups and direct booking.
LDG-05.Senior rate: A discount for older guests, with the qualifying age set by the hotel, and often for members of AARP, a membership group for older Americans.
LDG-05.Military rate: A discount offered to active-duty service members and often to veterans and their families.
LDG-05.Weekend rate: A price for Friday and Saturday nights. Business hotels often lower it because their corporate guests leave for the weekend.
LDG-05.Weekday rate: The price for Sunday to Thursday nights. Resorts often lower it midweek, when leisure demand is weaker.
LDG-05.Package rate: One price that bundles the room with extras such as meals, parking, spa treatments or attraction tickets.
LDG-05.Promotional rate: A temporary discounted price used to attract bookings during a slow period or to support a special offer.
LDG-05.Seasonal rate: A price that changes with the time of year, higher in peak season when demand is strong and lower in the off season.
LDG-05.Advance purchase rate: A discounted rate for guests who book and pay well ahead of arrival. It is usually non-refundable.
LDG-05.Best available rate: The lowest unrestricted rate open to the general public on a given night. It moves up and down with demand.
LDG-05.Walk-in rate: The price quoted to a guest who arrives without a reservation. It depends on how many rooms are still empty that night.
LDG-05.Family rate: A rate that lets children stay free or at a reduced price when sharing a room with their parents.
LDG-05.Extended-stay rate: A lower nightly price for guests who stay a long time, usually a week or more, often quoted by the week or month.
LDG-05.Employee rate: A deep discount for people who work for the hotel company, sometimes extended to their friends and family.
LDG-05.Last-minute rate: A reduced price offered close to the stay date to sell rooms that would otherwise go empty.
LDG-05.Student rate: A discount for students, and at some hotels teachers, who show valid school identification.
LDG-05.Special event rate: A rate set for dates around a big event or holiday. It is usually higher than normal because demand is strong.
LDG-05.Day rate: A price for using a room during the daytime only, without staying overnight, for example during a long layover.
LDG-05.Complimentary: A room given free of charge, often shortened to comp, for example to a VIP, a group organizer or a casino's big players.
LDG-05.Travel agent rate: A discount for travel agents and industry staff, offered so they get to know the hotel and recommend it to clients.
LDG-05.Airline rate: A low rate negotiated with an airline for its flight crews on layovers and for passengers stranded by canceled flights.
LDG-05.Opaque rate: A deep discount sold through a website that hides the hotel's name until after the guest has paid.
LDG-05.Meal plan rate: A room rate that includes meals. The American plan covers three meals a day, while the European plan includes no meals.

LDG-06.Free nights: Stays paid for with points instead of money. They are the main reward most members save toward.
LDG-06.Points: Credits earned for each dollar spent or night stayed, which members collect and later trade for rewards.
LDG-06.Room upgrades: A move to a better room or suite at no extra cost when one is available, usually for higher-level members.
LDG-06.Late checkout: Permission to keep the room past the normal departure time, for example until 2 p.m. or later.
LDG-06.Early check-in: Access to the room before the standard arrival time when one is ready, useful after an early flight.
LDG-06.Free breakfast: A morning meal included at no charge for members, usually those at higher levels, at hotels that normally charge for it.
LDG-06.Free Wi-Fi: Internet access at no charge for members, or a faster premium connection, at hotels that would otherwise bill for it.
LDG-06.Member rates: Lower prices that only members can book, usually on the hotel's own website. They reward joining and booking direct.
LDG-06.Elite status: Higher membership levels, such as gold or platinum, earned by staying more often. Each level adds more perks.
LDG-06.Bonus points: Extra points on top of the normal amount, given for special promotions or to members with higher status.
LDG-06.Priority check-in: A faster arrival, through a dedicated line or by checking in on a phone app and using the phone as the room key.
LDG-06.Lounge access: Entry to a private club lounge in the hotel that serves free snacks, drinks and often breakfast.
LDG-06.Welcome gift: A small present on arrival, such as bottled water, snacks, a drink or extra points.
LDG-06.Airline miles: The option to earn frequent flyer miles on hotel stays, or to convert hotel points into miles, with partner airlines.
LDG-06.Free parking: Parking at no charge for members, a real saving at city hotels where parking can cost a lot per night.
LDG-06.Dining and spa discounts: Reduced prices or credits to spend at the hotel's restaurants, bars and spa.
LDG-06.Personalized service: The hotel stores a member's preferences, such as room type, floor or pillow choice, and prepares for them before arrival.
LDG-06.Guaranteed room availability: A promise that top-level members can book a room even when the hotel is nearly sold out, if they reserve far enough ahead.
LDG-06.Partner discounts: Savings with companies linked to the program, such as car rental firms, airlines and cruise lines.
LDG-06.Priority customer service: A dedicated phone line or support team that handles higher-level members faster than general callers.
LDG-06.Exclusive experiences: Access to things money cannot easily buy, such as concert tickets, sporting events or private dinners, often paid for with points.
LDG-06.No blackout dates: A promise that members can use points for a free night on any date a standard room is available, even on busy days.
LDG-06.Gift cards and merchandise: The option to trade points for store gift cards or products instead of hotel stays.

LDG-07.Occupied: A guest is currently registered to the room, so it cannot be given to anyone else.
LDG-07.Vacant: No guest is registered to the room. It may or may not have been cleaned yet.
LDG-07.Clean: Housekeeping has finished servicing the room. A room that is both vacant and clean is ready to be assigned.
LDG-07.Dirty: The room needs to be cleaned before another guest can use it. A vacant dirty room is also said to be on change.
LDG-07.Out of order: The room cannot be sold because of a serious problem, such as major repairs or renovation, and is removed from the rooms available.
LDG-07.Do not disturb: The guest has asked not to be interrupted, often with a door sign, so housekeeping does not enter. Shortened to DND.
LDG-07.Checked out: The guest has paid the bill, returned the keys and left the hotel, so the room now needs cleaning.
LDG-07.Reserved: The room has been booked or set aside for a guest who has not yet arrived.
LDG-07.Stayover: The guest is not leaving today and will stay at least one more night, so the room gets a lighter daily service.
LDG-07.Due out: The guest is expected to check out today, so the room should soon be free for cleaning.
LDG-07.Late checkout: The guest has been allowed to leave after the normal check-out time, so the room will be ready later than usual.
LDG-07.Due in: A guest with a reservation is expected to arrive today, so a room must be ready in time.
LDG-07.No-show: A guest who had a reservation but never arrived and did not cancel, leaving a room that was held unsold.
LDG-07.Inspected: A supervisor has checked the cleaned room and confirmed it meets the hotel's standards, so it can be sold.
LDG-07.Out of service: The room has a small problem, such as a burnt-out bulb, and is briefly held back, but it can be returned to sale quickly.
LDG-07.Lockout: The room has been locked so the guest cannot get back in until they speak with management, often about an unpaid bill.
LDG-07.Blocked: The room is being held for a particular guest or group and should not be assigned to anyone else.
LDG-07.Make up room: The guest has asked for the room to be cleaned, often by hanging a sign on the door.
LDG-07.Complimentary: The room is occupied, but the guest is not being charged for it.
LDG-07.Sleep out: A guest is registered to the room but did not sleep in it, so the bed has not been used.
LDG-07.Skipper: A guest who has left the hotel without paying the bill.
LDG-07.Sleeper: The guest has paid and left, but the front desk did not update its records, so the empty room still shows as occupied.
LDG-07.Did not check out: The guest arranged to pay the bill, so is not a skipper, but left without telling the front desk. Shortened to DNCO.
LDG-07.Double locked: The door has been secured with the deadbolt from inside, so it cannot be opened with a standard room key.
LDG-07.House use: The room is being used by a hotel employee, such as a manager staying overnight, and earns no revenue.

LDG-08.Cleaning guest rooms: The department's core job: servicing each occupied room daily and fully cleaning rooms after guests check out.
LDG-08.Making beds: Stripping used sheets and remaking each bed neatly to the hotel's standard, one of the first things a guest notices.
LDG-08.Cleaning bathrooms: Scrubbing and disinfecting the toilet, sink, shower and floor. A dirty bathroom is one of the most common guest complaints.
LDG-08.Changing linens and towels: Removing used sheets and towels and replacing them with freshly laundered ones.
LDG-08.Vacuuming: Removing dirt from carpets and floors in rooms and hallways, done every time a room is serviced.
LDG-08.Emptying trash: Taking the trash out of the wastebaskets in each room and putting in clean liners.
LDG-08.Restocking amenities: Replacing the items guests use up, such as soap, shampoo, toilet paper, coffee and cups.
LDG-08.Dusting: Wiping dust from furniture, lamps, shelves and other surfaces so the room looks and feels clean.
LDG-08.Laundry: Washing, drying, pressing and folding the hotel's sheets, towels and uniforms, in the hotel's own laundry or through an outside service.
LDG-08.Sanitizing surfaces: Using disinfectant on things many hands touch, such as door handles, remote controls, phones and light switches, to kill germs.
LDG-08.Cleaning public areas: Keeping shared spaces such as the lobby, hallways, elevators and public restrooms clean throughout the day.
LDG-08.Reporting maintenance problems: Telling the engineering department about anything broken, such as a leaking faucet or a dead bulb, so it is fixed before the next guest.
LDG-08.Cleaning windows and mirrors: Wiping glass until it is free of streaks, smears and fingerprints.
LDG-08.Inspecting rooms: A supervisor checks cleaned rooms against the hotel's standards before they are released for sale.
LDG-08.Handling lost and found: Collecting and logging items guests leave behind in rooms and storing them safely until they are claimed.
LDG-08.Updating room status: Telling the front desk which rooms are clean, dirty or out of order, so guests are only sent to rooms that are ready.
LDG-08.Delivering guest requests: Bringing items guests ask for, such as extra towels, pillows, blankets or toiletries, to their rooms.
LDG-08.Stocking housekeeping carts: Loading each attendant's cart with the linens, supplies and cleaning products needed for the rooms assigned that shift.
LDG-08.Turndown service: An evening visit to fold back the bed covers, tidy the room and close the curtains so it is ready for sleep.
LDG-08.Deep cleaning: Thorough cleaning done from time to time rather than daily, such as shampooing carpets, washing curtains and turning mattresses.
LDG-08.Managing linen inventory: Counting and controlling the stock of sheets and towels so there is always enough clean linen for every room.
LDG-08.Setting up cribs and rollaway beds: Delivering and setting up baby cribs and folding extra beds in rooms where guests have requested them.
LDG-08.Key control: Signing master keys in and out and keeping track of them, because a lost master key puts every guest room at risk.

LDG-09.Business travelers: People traveling for work. They stay mostly on weekdays, book late and care about location, Wi-Fi and a place to work.
LDG-09.Leisure travelers: People traveling for vacation or fun. They stay mostly on weekends and holidays and tend to be more sensitive to price.
LDG-09.Families: Parents traveling with children, who look for larger rooms, a pool, free breakfast and good value.
LDG-09.Groups: Ten or more rooms booked together under one contract, for example a tour bus party, usually at a discounted rate.
LDG-09.Convention attendees: People in town for a conference, trade show or meeting. They fill many rooms at once and also use the hotel's meeting space.
LDG-09.Wedding parties: Guests attending a wedding who book a block of rooms, often along with a reception in the hotel's ballroom.
LDG-09.Couples: Two adults traveling together, often on a romantic trip or honeymoon, who are drawn to packages, spas and fine dining.
LDG-09.Sports teams: Teams, with their coaches and families, traveling to games or tournaments. They need many rooms close together.
LDG-09.Government travelers: Public employees and military personnel on official trips, whose spending is capped at a set daily allowance.
LDG-09.Extended-stay guests: People who need a room for weeks or months, such as workers on a long project or families who are relocating.
LDG-09.International travelers: Visitors from other countries, who often stay longer, spend more and may need language help or currency exchange.
LDG-09.Seniors: Older and retired travelers, who have flexible schedules and can travel midweek and in the off season.
LDG-09.Budget travelers: Guests whose main concern is a low price and who will give up extras to get one.
LDG-09.Luxury travelers: Wealthy guests who will pay high rates for top-quality rooms, personal service and exclusive experiences.
LDG-09.Event attendees: People in town for a concert, festival or big game, who create short bursts of very high demand.
LDG-09.Airline crews: Pilots and flight attendants on layovers. Airlines sign contracts for rooms every night, giving the hotel steady low-rate business.
LDG-09.Transient guests: Individual travelers who book on their own, not as part of a group or contract, often for short stays.
LDG-09.Young travelers: Students and young adults, who usually have smaller budgets and value social spaces, technology and unique experiences.
LDG-09.Solo travelers: People traveling alone, who value safety, a single room at a fair price and chances to meet others.
LDG-09.Local residents: People who live nearby and book a short break close to home, called a staycation, or use the restaurant and spa.
LDG-09.Association groups: Members of professional or trade organizations who gather for regular meetings and annual conventions.
LDG-09.Loyalty members: Guests enrolled in the brand's rewards program, who return often and tend to book directly with the hotel.
LDG-09.Bleisure travelers: Guests who mix business and leisure by adding vacation days to a work trip, sometimes bringing family along.
LDG-09.SMERF groups: Social, military, educational, religious and fraternal groups. They watch prices closely and often fill slow periods.
LDG-09.Distressed passengers: Airline customers stranded overnight by a canceled or delayed flight. The airline often pays for their rooms.
LDG-09.Pet owners: Guests traveling with a dog or cat, who look for hotels that allow animals and may pay an extra fee.
LDG-09.Medical travelers: Patients and their families who stay near a hospital or clinic during treatment, often for several nights.
LDG-09.Digital nomads: People who work online from anywhere and stay for long periods, needing fast Wi-Fi and a good workspace.

RFS-01.Fast food: Also called quick service. Customers order and pay at a counter or drive-through and get low-priced food within minutes.
RFS-01.Fine dining: The highest level of full service, with expert staff, top-quality food, a formal setting and high prices.
RFS-01.Casual dining: A sit-down restaurant with table service, a relaxed atmosphere and moderate prices.
RFS-01.Full-service restaurant: Any restaurant where guests are seated and a server takes the order and brings the food to the table.
RFS-01.Fast casual: A step above fast food. Guests order at a counter but get fresher, higher-quality food at somewhat higher prices.
RFS-01.Buffet: Guests pay one price and serve themselves from a long display of dishes, usually as much as they want.
RFS-01.Family restaurant: A casual sit-down restaurant with a broad, moderately priced menu, kids' meals and often little or no alcohol.
RFS-01.Cafe: A small, informal place centered on coffee and other drinks, with light food such as pastries and sandwiches.
RFS-01.Food truck: A vehicle fitted with a kitchen that travels to where customers are and sells food through a window.
RFS-01.Diner: A casual restaurant with a long counter and booths, serving simple comfort food and often breakfast all day.
RFS-01.Cafeteria: Guests carry a tray along a serving line, choose dishes from behind the counter and pay at the end.
RFS-01.Pizzeria: A restaurant that specializes in pizza, sold whole or by the slice to eat in, take out or have delivered.
RFS-01.Bistro: A small, informal restaurant, French in origin, serving simple, hearty dishes at moderate prices.
RFS-01.Pub: A bar that also serves casual food. A gastropub puts extra focus on the quality of its menu.
RFS-01.Bakery: A shop that bakes and sells bread, cakes and pastries. A bakery cafe adds seating, coffee and light meals.
RFS-01.Deli: Short for delicatessen. A shop that sells made-to-order sandwiches, sliced meats, cheeses and prepared salads.
RFS-01.Pop-up restaurant: A temporary restaurant that opens for a short time in a borrowed space, often to test a concept or a chef's ideas.
RFS-01.Takeout restaurant: A restaurant with little or no seating that prepares food for customers to carry out and eat elsewhere.
RFS-01.Food stand: A small booth, cart or kiosk selling a limited menu, such as a concession stand at a stadium or a street vendor.
RFS-01.Theme restaurant: A restaurant where the decor, staff and menu follow a concept such as a rainforest or movies, making the experience the main draw.
RFS-01.Upscale casual: Sits between casual and fine dining, with better food and decor than a casual chain but a relaxed feel.
RFS-01.Drive-in: Customers park and eat in their cars, with food brought out to them, sometimes by servers called carhops.
RFS-01.Ice cream parlor: A shop that sells ice cream, sundaes, shakes and similar frozen desserts.
RFS-01.Catering: A business that prepares food and serves it at the client's event, either at its own hall or at another location.
RFS-01.Ghost kitchen: A kitchen that prepares food for delivery only. It has no dining room and takes orders through apps.
RFS-01.Food hall: A large shared space where many independent food vendors operate stalls around common seating.
RFS-01.Contract food service: A company hired to run the dining operations inside another organization, such as a school, hospital or office.
RFS-01.Supper club: A dining venue that combines a set dinner with a social evening, often with entertainment and sometimes a membership.

RFS-02.Executive chef: The head of the kitchen, who plans the menu, orders food, controls costs and manages all the kitchen staff.
RFS-02.Line cook: Cooks orders at one station on the cooking line, such as the grill or saute station. Called a chef de partie in French.
RFS-02.Dishwasher: Cleans dishes, glasses, pots and utensils and helps keep the kitchen clean, so cooks and servers never run short.
RFS-02.Sous chef: The second in command, who supervises the cooks day to day and runs the kitchen when the executive chef is away.
RFS-02.Prep cook: Gets ingredients ready before service by washing, chopping, measuring and portioning them for the line cooks.
RFS-02.Pastry chef: Makes desserts, pastries and other baked sweets. The French title is patissier.
RFS-02.Baker: Makes breads, rolls and other baked goods, often working very early so they are fresh for service.
RFS-02.Kitchen manager: Runs the business side of the kitchen in restaurants without an executive chef, handling ordering, schedules and food cost.
RFS-02.Grill cook: Cooks foods such as steaks, burgers and chicken on the grill. The French brigade title is grillardin.
RFS-02.Fry cook: Runs the deep fryers, cooking foods such as fries, chicken and fish. Called friturier in the brigade system.
RFS-02.Expediter: Stands between the kitchen and dining room, calling out orders, checking each plate and making sure a table's food leaves together.
RFS-02.Short-order cook: Quickly cooks simple foods to order, such as eggs, burgers and sandwiches, as in a diner.
RFS-02.Saucier: The cook in charge of sauces and sauteed dishes, traditionally one of the most skilled stations in the brigade.
RFS-02.Fish cook: Prepares and cooks fish and seafood dishes. The French brigade title is poissonnier.
RFS-02.Pizza cook: Stretches dough, adds toppings and bakes pizzas. The Italian term is pizzaiolo.
RFS-02.Sushi chef: Prepares sushi and sashimi, which takes special training in cutting raw fish and making seasoned rice.
RFS-02.Banquet chef: Leads the cooking for large catered events, where hundreds of identical meals must be ready at the same time.
RFS-02.Garde manger: The pantry chef, who runs the cold station and prepares salads, cold appetizers, dressings and cured meats.
RFS-02.Butcher: Cuts and portions meat, poultry and sometimes fish for the other stations. Called boucher in French.
RFS-02.Roast cook: Prepares roasted and braised meats and their gravies. The French brigade title is rotisseur.
RFS-02.Roundsman: A swing cook who can work any station and fills in wherever someone is absent. Called tournant in French.
RFS-02.Vegetable cook: Prepares vegetables, soups, starches and egg dishes. The French brigade title is entremetier.
RFS-02.Commis: A junior cook who works under a station chef to learn that station's work.
RFS-02.Receiving clerk: Checks deliveries against the order for quantity and quality, then stores the goods. A back-of-house job, though not a cooking one.

RFS-03.Server: Takes guests' orders, brings food and drinks, checks on the table and presents the bill.
RFS-03.Host: Greets guests at the door, manages the waiting list and reservations, and seats parties so tables are spread evenly among servers.
RFS-03.Bartender: Mixes and serves drinks at the bar, both for guests seated there and for servers' tables.
RFS-03.Busser: Clears and resets tables, refills water and helps servers, so tables are ready quickly for the next guests.
RFS-03.Manager: Oversees the dining room during service, supervises staff, handles guest complaints and makes sure the shift runs smoothly.
RFS-03.Cashier: Rings up orders and takes payment at a register, common in quick-service and counter-service restaurants.
RFS-03.Food runner: Carries finished plates from the kitchen to the right table, so food arrives hot and servers can stay with their guests.
RFS-03.Barista: Prepares and serves coffee drinks such as espresso and lattes, usually at a cafe counter.
RFS-03.Sommelier: A trained wine expert who builds the wine list and helps guests choose wines that suit their meal.
RFS-03.Maitre d: Short for maitre d'hotel. The head of the dining room, who manages reservations, greets guests and supervises the service staff.
RFS-03.Cocktail server: Takes drink orders and serves guests in a bar or lounge area away from the bar itself.
RFS-03.Delivery driver: Brings orders from the restaurant to customers' homes or workplaces and often collects payment.
RFS-03.Barback: The bartender's assistant, who restocks ice, glasses, bottles and garnishes and keeps the bar clean.
RFS-03.Drive-through attendant: Takes orders through a speaker, collects payment and hands food to customers in their cars.
RFS-03.Counter attendant: Takes orders, serves food and often handles payment from behind a counter instead of at tables.
RFS-03.Takeout specialist: Handles to-go orders: taking them by phone or online, checking and packing them, and handing them to customers.
RFS-03.Banquet server: Serves food and drinks to large groups at catered events such as weddings and conferences.
RFS-03.Bar manager: Runs the bar operation, including ordering drinks, controlling stock, creating the drink menu and supervising bartenders.
RFS-03.Event coordinator: Books and plans private parties and group events at the restaurant, working out the menu and details with the client.
RFS-03.Valet: Parks guests' cars on arrival and brings them back when the guests leave, a service at many upscale restaurants.
RFS-03.Captain: A senior server in a fine dining room who leads a team of servers and is responsible for a section of tables.
RFS-03.Coat check attendant: Takes guests' coats and bags, stores them safely and returns them in exchange for a claim ticket.
RFS-03.Reservationist: Answers calls and online requests to book tables and keeps the reservation book accurate.
RFS-03.Bouncer: Checks identification at the door and handles unruly guests, mostly at bars and restaurants with nightlife.
RFS-03.Carhop: A server at a drive-in restaurant who takes orders and brings food out to customers in their parked cars.

RFS-04.A la carte: A menu on which every item is listed and priced separately, so guests build their own meal.
RFS-04.Kids menu: A short menu of smaller portions and simple dishes at lower prices, aimed at children.
RFS-04.Breakfast menu: A list of morning dishes, such as eggs, pancakes and cereal, offered during breakfast hours.
RFS-04.Lunch menu: Dishes offered at midday, usually lighter, faster to serve and cheaper than those at dinner.
RFS-04.Dinner menu: The evening menu, usually with larger portions, more courses and higher prices than lunch.
RFS-04.Dessert menu: A separate list of sweets, and often coffee, handed to guests after the main course.
RFS-04.Drink menu: A list of beverages such as cocktails, beer, soft drinks and coffee, kept separate from the food menu.
RFS-04.Prix fixe: French for fixed price. A complete meal of several courses sold for one set price. Also called table d'hote.
RFS-04.Du jour menu: French for of the day. A list of dishes that changes daily, such as the daily specials.
RFS-04.Wine list: A menu of the wines a restaurant sells, usually grouped by type or region with prices by the glass and bottle.
RFS-04.Brunch menu: A late-morning menu that mixes breakfast and lunch dishes, most often served on weekends.
RFS-04.Value menu: A group of low-priced items or combo meals, used by quick-service restaurants to attract customers watching their budgets.
RFS-04.Seasonal menu: A menu that changes through the year to feature ingredients when they are freshest and cheapest.
RFS-04.Tasting menu: A series of many small courses chosen by the chef to show off the kitchen's skills, served for a set price.
RFS-04.Cycle menu: A set of menus that repeats over a fixed period, such as every four weeks. Common in schools and hospitals.
RFS-04.Static menu: A menu that offers the same items every day, as at most chain restaurants.
RFS-04.Takeout menu: A list of items available to go, often a printed sheet or web page customers keep for ordering later.
RFS-04.Happy hour menu: Discounted drinks and snacks offered during a set slow period, usually late afternoon, to bring in customers.
RFS-04.Catering menu: A list of dishes and packages for events, usually priced per person or by the tray.
RFS-04.Room service menu: The menu a hotel places in guest rooms, listing food that can be ordered and delivered to the room.
RFS-04.Digital menu: A menu shown on a screen, such as a menu board, a tablet or a phone after scanning a QR code. It is easy to update.
RFS-04.Combination menu: A menu that mixes pricing styles, for example a main dish priced with its sides while appetizers and desserts are priced separately.
RFS-04.Dietary menu: A menu for guests with particular needs, such as vegetarian, vegan, gluten-free or allergen-free choices.
RFS-04.Holiday menu: A special menu offered for one occasion, such as Thanksgiving or Valentine's Day, often at a set price.
RFS-04.Late-night menu: A shorter menu of items that are easy to prepare, offered after the main kitchen has closed.
RFS-04.Senior menu: Smaller portions at reduced prices offered to older guests.
RFS-04.California menu: A menu that lists breakfast, lunch and dinner items together and makes all of them available at any time of day.
RFS-04.Secret menu: Items that are not printed on the menu but that staff will make for customers who know to ask.
RFS-04.Market menu: A menu built around whatever fresh ingredients are available from the market or local farms, so it changes often.
RFS-04.Appetizer menu: A list of small dishes served before the main course or shared at the table, such as starters, small plates or tapas.

RFS-05.Table service: Guests sit at a table and a server takes the order and brings the food. It needs more staff than other styles.
RFS-05.Buffet service: Food is set out on a long table or display and guests walk up and serve themselves, so few servers are needed.
RFS-05.Takeout: Food is packed for customers to collect and eat somewhere else, so the restaurant needs little or no seating.
RFS-05.Drive-through: Customers order, pay and collect their food at windows without leaving their cars.
RFS-05.Delivery: Food is brought to the customer's home or workplace by the restaurant's own drivers or an outside delivery app.
RFS-05.Counter service: Guests order and pay at a counter, then carry the food to a table themselves or take it away.
RFS-05.Family-style service: Food is brought to the table on large platters and bowls, and guests pass them around and serve themselves.
RFS-05.Self-service: Guests help themselves to food or drinks, as at a salad bar or drink station, instead of being served by staff.
RFS-05.Cafeteria service: Guests move along a serving line with a tray while staff dish up the items they choose, then pay at the end.
RFS-05.American service: Food is portioned and arranged on plates in the kitchen, then carried to guests. It is the fastest and most common table service.
RFS-05.Curbside pickup: Customers order ahead, park outside and have a staff member bring the food out to the car.
RFS-05.Room service: Hotel guests order from a menu in the room and staff deliver the meal there on a tray or cart.
RFS-05.French service: A formal style in which servers finish, carve or cook dishes on a rolling cart, called a gueridon, beside the guests' table.
RFS-05.Banquet service: Serving a large group the same set meal at the same time, as at a wedding or conference dinner.
RFS-05.Catering: Preparing food and serving it at a client's event, either in the caterer's own space or at another location.
RFS-05.Russian service: Food is arranged on platters in the kitchen, and servers carry them to the table and place a portion on each guest's plate.
RFS-05.Butler service: Servers walk among standing guests carrying trays of small bites or drinks, and guests help themselves. Common at receptions.
RFS-05.Food stations: Separate tables around the room each offer one kind of food, such as carving or pasta, often prepared by a cook as guests watch.
RFS-05.Online ordering: Guests place and pay for orders through a website, app or kiosk instead of telling a staff member.
RFS-05.Tray service: Complete meals are assembled on trays and carried to people who cannot come to a dining room, such as hospital patients.
RFS-05.Vending: Food and drinks sold from machines with no staff present, available at any hour.
RFS-05.Carhop service: At a drive-in, servers called carhops take orders from customers in parked cars and bring the food out to them.

RFS-06.Handwashing: Washing hands with soap and warm running water, taking at least 20 seconds in all, before handling food and after using the restroom or touching raw meat.
RFS-06.Cooking to safe temperatures: Heating food until its inside reaches the minimum temperature that kills harmful germs, for example 165 degrees Fahrenheit for poultry.
RFS-06.Holding food at safe temperatures: Keeping cold food at 41 degrees Fahrenheit or below and hot food at 135 or above, outside the danger zone where bacteria grow fast.
RFS-06.Preventing cross-contamination: Keeping germs from spreading between foods, for example by using separate cutting boards for raw meat and ready-to-eat food.
RFS-06.Wearing gloves: Using single-use gloves when touching ready-to-eat food and changing them between tasks, so bare hands do not pass on germs.
RFS-06.Cleaning and sanitizing: Cleaning removes visible dirt and food, and sanitizing then reduces germs to safe levels. Surfaces that touch food need both.
RFS-06.Hair restraints: Hairnets, hats or beard covers that keep hair from falling into food.
RFS-06.Checking temperatures: Using a calibrated food thermometer to measure food and writing the readings in a log, so unsafe food is caught early.
RFS-06.Proper food storage: Keeping food covered, off the floor and in the right order, with raw meat on shelves below ready-to-eat food so it cannot drip on it.
RFS-06.Personal hygiene: Staff habits that keep germs out of food, such as clean uniforms, short nails, covered cuts and no jewelry.
RFS-06.FIFO: First in, first out. Older stock is placed in front and used before newer stock, so food is used while it is still fresh.
RFS-06.Date labeling: Marking containers with what the food is and when it was prepared or must be thrown out, so nothing is kept too long.
RFS-06.Food safety training: Teaching staff safe food handling, often through a certification course such as ServSafe or a food handler card.
RFS-06.Washing produce: Rinsing fruits and vegetables under running water before cutting or serving them to remove dirt and germs.
RFS-06.Discarding expired food: Throwing away food that is past its use-by date or shows signs of spoilage instead of serving it.
RFS-06.Proper dishwashing: Washing, rinsing and sanitizing dishes and utensils, by machine or in a three-compartment sink, then letting them air dry.
RFS-06.Health inspections: Checks of the kitchen against the food safety code, done by the local health department or by managers as self-inspections.
RFS-06.HACCP plan: Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Points. A written system that finds the steps where food could become unsafe and sets controls for each.
RFS-06.Excluding sick employees: Keeping workers with symptoms such as vomiting, diarrhea or jaundice (yellowing skin or eyes) out of the kitchen, because they can easily infect customers.
RFS-06.Pest control: Keeping out insects and rodents, which carry disease, by sealing gaps, removing trash and using a licensed pest control operator.
RFS-06.Allergen controls: Steps that protect guests with food allergies, such as separate equipment, clear labeling and staff who know every ingredient.
RFS-06.Inspecting deliveries: Checking incoming food for correct temperature, damaged packaging and signs of spoilage, and rejecting anything unsafe.
RFS-06.Time limits on food left out: Limiting how long food sits in the danger zone. Food held without temperature control is generally thrown out after four hours.
RFS-06.Rapid cooling: Chilling hot food quickly, to 70 degrees Fahrenheit within two hours and then to 41 within four more, using ice baths or shallow pans.
RFS-06.Proper thawing: Defrosting frozen food safely in a refrigerator, under cold running water, in a microwave or during cooking, never on the counter.
RFS-06.Proper reheating: Bringing previously cooked food that will be held hot back up to 165 degrees Fahrenheit quickly, within two hours.
RFS-06.Approved suppliers: Buying food only from reputable, inspected sources that follow food safety laws, so it arrives safe.
RFS-06.Storing chemicals away from food: Keeping cleaners and sanitizers labeled and in a separate area, so they cannot spill into or be mistaken for food.

RFS-07.Food cost percentage: The cost of the food used divided by food sales. Many restaurants aim to keep it at roughly 28 to 35 percent.
RFS-07.Labor cost: What the restaurant spends on wages, payroll taxes and benefits, usually tracked as a percentage of sales.
RFS-07.Sales: The total money taken in from guests over a period. It is the starting point for almost every other measure.
RFS-07.Profit margin: The share of sales left as profit after all expenses are paid. Restaurant margins are typically only a few percent.
RFS-07.Average check: Total sales divided by the number of guests or checks, showing how much each guest typically spends.
RFS-07.Table turnover: The number of times a table is used by a new party during a meal period. Faster turns mean more sales from the same seats.
RFS-07.Guest count: The number of people served in a period. Each guest served is called a cover.
RFS-07.Beverage cost: The cost of the drinks sold divided by beverage sales. For alcohol it is often called pour cost.
RFS-07.Customer satisfaction: How happy guests are with the food and service, measured through reviews, ratings and surveys.
RFS-07.Overhead: Ongoing costs that are not tied to a particular dish, such as rent, utilities and insurance.
RFS-07.Food waste: Food that is thrown out because it spoiled, was over-prepared or was cooked wrongly. Every wasted item raises food cost.
RFS-07.Inventory turnover: How many times the stock of food is used up and replaced in a period. Slow turnover suggests over-ordering and risk of spoilage.
RFS-07.Employee turnover: The rate at which staff quit and must be replaced. It is high in restaurants and adds hiring and training costs.
RFS-07.Total expenses: The sum of everything the restaurant spends to operate, which must stay below sales for the business to earn a profit.
RFS-07.Cost of goods sold: The cost of the food and drink actually used to make what was sold. It equals opening inventory plus purchases minus closing inventory.
RFS-07.Inventory: The quantity and value of food, drink and supplies on hand. Too much ties up cash and spoils, and too little causes shortages.
RFS-07.Supply costs: Spending on non-food items such as napkins, takeout containers, cleaning products and small equipment.
RFS-07.Prime cost: Cost of goods sold plus total labor cost. It is the largest and most controllable part of a restaurant's spending.
RFS-07.Contribution margin: A menu item's selling price minus the cost of its ingredients, the amount each sale adds toward other costs and profit.
RFS-07.Gross profit: Sales minus the cost of goods sold, the money left to cover labor, rent and all other expenses.
RFS-07.Sales mix: The share of total sales that comes from each menu item, showing which dishes are popular and which are not.
RFS-07.Break-even point: The level of sales at which total revenue exactly equals total costs, so the restaurant makes neither a profit nor a loss.
RFS-07.Speed of service: How long guests wait for their food, often measured as ticket time from order to delivery.
RFS-07.Marketing costs: Money spent on advertising, promotions and social media to bring in customers.
RFS-07.Repeat customers: The share of guests who come back. Regulars cost less to attract than new customers and give steadier sales.
RFS-07.Delivery and online sales: Revenue from orders placed through apps and websites, tracked along with the fees that delivery companies charge.
RFS-07.RevPASH: Revenue per available seat hour. Sales divided by the number of seats times the hours open, showing how well seats are used.
RFS-07.Sales per labor hour: Total sales divided by the hours staff worked, a measure of how productive the scheduled team was.
RFS-07.Food cost variance: The gap between what food should have cost, based on recipes and items sold, and what it actually cost. It reveals waste or theft.
RFS-07.Comps and voids: Comps are items given away free and voids are items canceled from a check. Managers track both to catch errors and theft.
RFS-07.Same-store sales: Sales at locations open at least a year compared with the same period a year earlier, showing true growth without new openings.
RFS-07.Sales per square foot: Total sales divided by the restaurant's floor area, showing how well the space earns money.

RFS-08.Peanuts: A legume, not a true nut, that causes some of the most severe allergic reactions. It hides in sauces, baked goods and frying oil.
RFS-08.Milk: Cow's milk and products made from it, such as cheese, butter and cream. A milk allergy is different from lactose intolerance.
RFS-08.Eggs: Found in the obvious dishes and also in baked goods, pasta, mayonnaise and many sauces.
RFS-08.Tree nuts: Nuts that grow on trees, such as almonds, walnuts, pecans and cashews. They are a separate allergen from peanuts.
RFS-08.Shellfish: Crustaceans such as shrimp, crab and lobster. This is one of the most common food allergies among adults.
RFS-08.Wheat: The grain used in most flour, bread, pasta and breading. It also appears as a thickener in soups and sauces.
RFS-08.Fish: Finned fish such as salmon, tuna and cod. It can hide in items such as Caesar dressing and Worcestershire sauce.
RFS-08.Soy: Soybeans and foods made from them, such as tofu, soy sauce and edamame. Soy is also common in processed foods.
RFS-08.Sesame: Sesame seeds, sesame oil and tahini. It became the ninth major allergen under United States law in 2023.

RFS-09.Portion control: Serving the same measured amount every time, using scales, scoops and ladles, so no plate costs more than planned.
RFS-09.Reducing food waste: Cutting the amount of food thrown away through spoilage, over-preparation and mistakes, often by recording it in a waste log.
