SPE-08.Royalties: Payments made each time a creative work is sold, streamed or broadcast, such as a song or a rerun of a television show.
SPE-08.Own business ventures: Profits from companies the star starts or owns, such as a clothing line, a restaurant or a production company.
SPE-08.Licensing their name and likeness: Fees for permission to use the star's name or image, for example in a video game or on trading cards.
SPE-08.Acting and media work: Pay for roles in films and television, hosting shows, podcasts or working as a commentator.
SPE-08.Speaking engagements: Fees for giving talks to companies, schools and conferences, often about motivation or their career.
SPE-08.Autograph signings: Payment for signing items at shows and events, or for signing memorabilia that dealers then sell.
SPE-08.Camps and clinics: Fees from training camps and lessons run under the star's name for young athletes or students.
SPE-08.Book deals: An advance and royalties from a publisher for a memoir or other book, often written with a professional writer.
SPE-08.Investments: Returns from putting money into stocks, property or shares of companies, sometimes taken in place of cash from a sponsor.
SPE-08.Personalized video messages: Fees fans pay for a short custom video greeting from the star, through services such as Cameo.
SPE-08.Pension and deferred pay: Money paid out later. Leagues fund retirement plans for players, and some contracts delay part of the salary for years.

SPE-09.Box office: Money from tickets sold at movie theaters. The studio and the theater owner each keep a share of every ticket.
SPE-09.Streaming rights: Fees a streaming service pays to carry the film, or the value it brings to the studio's own service by attracting subscribers.
SPE-09.Merchandise: Royalties from toys, clothing and other products based on the film. For some franchises this earns more than ticket sales.
SPE-09.DVD and Blu-ray sales: Sales of physical discs for watching at home, once a huge source of income and now much smaller.
SPE-09.Digital rentals and purchases: Fees viewers pay to rent or buy the film online, known as video on demand.
SPE-09.Television rights: Fees paid by broadcast and cable networks for the right to show the film on their channels.
SPE-09.International distribution: Income from releasing the film in other countries, through the studio's own offices or by selling rights to local distributors.
SPE-09.Product placement: Fees brands pay to have their products shown or used on screen within the film.
SPE-09.Soundtrack sales: Income from sales, streams and licensing of the film's songs and score.
SPE-09.Promotional tie-ins: Deals with partners such as fast food chains that pay to link their products to the film and help advertise it.
SPE-09.Video game adaptations: Fees and royalties from game makers licensed to create games based on the film.
SPE-09.Sequels and spin-offs: Further films and series built on a successful original, which earn new income from the same characters and world.
SPE-09.Theatrical re-releases: Bringing an older film back to theaters, often for an anniversary or in a new format, to sell tickets again.
SPE-09.Theme park attractions: Rides and themed areas based on the film, either in the studio's own parks or licensed to other park operators.
SPE-09.Airline and hotel licensing: Fees for showing the film outside theaters and homes, such as on flights, on cruise ships and in hotel rooms.
SPE-09.Book and comic tie-ins: Royalties from novelizations, comics and art books that publishers produce under license from the studio.
SPE-09.Stage adaptations: Income from turning the film into a live stage show, such as a Broadway musical.

HT-08.Slow service: Guests wait too long to be seated, served, checked in or helped. Long waits are among the most frequent complaints in both hotels and restaurants.
HT-08.Rude staff: Employees who are unfriendly, impatient or dismissive. Guests often remember how they were treated longer than what they bought.
HT-08.Dirty room: A guest room, restroom, table or dish that is not clean. Cleanliness is one of the first things guests judge a business on.
HT-08.Wrong order: The guest receives a different dish than the one ordered, or part of the order is missing, usually because of a mistake in taking or passing on the order.
HT-08.Poor food quality: Food that arrives cold, overcooked, undercooked, stale or simply not tasty, so the guest feels the meal was not worth the price.
HT-08.Noise: Sound from other guests, hallways, traffic or music that stops a hotel guest from sleeping or a diner from holding a conversation.
HT-08.High prices: The guest feels the room, meal or extras cost more than they were worth. This is a complaint about value, not only about the price itself.
HT-08.Billing errors: Mistakes on the check or the room bill, such as a charge for something the guest never had or the same charge posted twice.
HT-08.Room not ready: The guest arrives at check-in time and the room has not been cleaned or released yet, so the stay begins with a wait.
HT-08.Broken equipment: Something in the room or building does not work, such as the air conditioning, the hot water, the television or an elevator.
HT-08.Wi-Fi problems: Wireless internet that is slow, keeps dropping or will not connect. Guests now expect it to work as reliably as the lights.
HT-08.Lost reservation: The business has no record of the booking, or recorded the wrong date, room type or party size, so the guest's plans are upset on arrival.
HT-08.Uncomfortable room temperature: A guest room or dining room that is too hot or too cold, often because the heating or cooling is hard to control.
HT-08.Inattentive service: Staff do not notice or check on the guest, so drinks go unfilled, requests are forgotten and the guest feels ignored.
HT-08.Uncomfortable bed: A mattress or pillows that are too hard, too soft or worn out. Sleep is the main thing a hotel sells, so this complaint matters.
HT-08.Misleading advertising: The room, view or meal does not match the photos or description the guest saw before buying, so the guest feels misled.
HT-08.Pests: Insects or rodents, such as bed bugs, cockroaches or mice, seen in a guest room or dining area. Even one sighting can ruin a reputation.
HT-08.Hidden fees: Charges the guest did not expect, such as a resort fee or a parking fee, that make the final bill higher than the advertised price.
HT-08.Foreign object in food: Something in a dish that should not be there, such as a hair, an insect or a piece of packaging.
HT-08.Unpleasant odors: Bad smells such as cigarette smoke, mildew or strong cleaning chemicals in a room, hallway or dining area.
HT-08.Small portions: Servings the guest thinks are too small for the price paid, which makes the meal feel like poor value.
HT-08.Overbooking: The hotel accepted more reservations than it has rooms, so a guest with a booking is sent, or walked, to another hotel.
HT-08.Missing amenities: Items or facilities the guest expected are not there or are closed, such as towels, toiletries, the pool or the fitness center.
HT-08.Menu items unavailable: The kitchen has run out of a dish or drink listed on the menu, so the guest cannot order what they came for.
HT-08.Parking problems: Too few parking spaces, a lot that is far from the entrance, or a parking charge the guest thinks is too high.
HT-08.Safety concerns: The guest does not feel safe, for example because of poor lighting, a broken lock, strangers in the hallways or a theft from a room.

HT-09.Apology: A sincere statement that the business is sorry for what went wrong. It costs nothing and is the first step in any service recovery.
HT-09.Refund: Returning all or part of what the guest paid for a room, meal or service that fell short.
HT-09.Free meal: Taking the cost of a meal off the check so the guest pays nothing for it. Staff call this comping the meal.
HT-09.Discount: Lowering the price of the meal or the room rate by a set amount or percentage, when a full refund would be more than the problem calls for.
HT-09.Free dessert or drink: A small extra item given at no charge, such as a dessert, an appetizer or a drink. It is a common gesture after a long wait or a minor mistake.
HT-09.Replace the dish: Cooking the order again, correctly and quickly, when a dish arrives wrong, cold or badly prepared.
HT-09.Room upgrade: Moving the guest to a better class of room, such as a suite or a room with a view, at no extra charge.
HT-09.Room change: Moving the guest to a different room when the first one is noisy, dirty or has something broken that cannot be fixed quickly.
HT-09.Voucher for a future visit: A coupon for a free or discounted meal or stay next time. It makes up for the problem and also gives the guest a reason to return.
HT-09.Gift card: A card loaded with a set amount of money that the guest can spend at the business on a later visit.
HT-09.Free night: Removing the charge for one night of the stay, or offering a night free on a later visit, after a serious problem with a hotel room.
HT-09.Fix the problem: Putting right the thing that went wrong, at once, such as sending maintenance to repair the air conditioning or bringing the missing towels.
HT-09.Manager visit: Having a manager come to speak with the guest in person, which shows that the business takes the complaint seriously.
HT-09.Loyalty points: Extra points added to the guest's loyalty program account, which can be traded later for free nights or other rewards.
HT-09.Waived fee or charge: Removing one charge from the bill, such as a resort fee, a parking fee or the price of the item the guest complained about.
HT-09.Follow-up contact: Calling, visiting or writing to the guest afterward to make sure the problem was solved and the guest is now satisfied.
HT-09.Gift sent to the room: A small present delivered to the guest room as an apology, such as a fruit plate, chocolates or a bottle of wine. Hotels call it an amenity.
HT-09.Free breakfast: Breakfast in the hotel restaurant at no charge, often given as a voucher after a problem with the room the night before.
HT-09.Late checkout: Letting the guest keep the room past the normal checkout time without a fee, a gesture that costs the hotel very little.
HT-09.Handwritten note: A short personal letter of apology from a manager, left in the room or sent after the stay, which shows the guest was not forgotten.
HT-09.Free parking: Taking the parking or valet charge off the bill for the stay or the visit.
HT-09.Priority service: Moving the guest to the front of the line, for example by seating the party next or having the kitchen rush the order, after a long wait.
HT-09.Paid room at another hotel: When a hotel is overbooked and has no room for a guest with a reservation, it finds and pays for a room at a nearby hotel. The trade calls this walking the guest.
HT-09.Free spa treatment or activity: A treatment, a round of golf or a credit to spend at the resort, given at no charge to make up for a serious disappointment.
HT-09.Pay for cleaning or damage: Covering the guest's cost when the business caused it, such as the dry cleaning bill after a server spills a drink on a guest's clothes.

HT-10.Point-of-sale system: The computerized register where staff enter orders and take payment. Often shortened to POS, it also records every sale for management reports.
HT-10.Online reservation system: Software on a website or app that lets guests book a room or a table themselves at any hour and see what is available.
HT-10.Wi-Fi: Wireless internet access. Guests expect it for their own devices, and staff rely on it for tablets, card readers and other equipment.
HT-10.Mobile app: A program on a guest's phone for tasks such as booking, checking in, ordering, paying and collecting loyalty rewards.
HT-10.Key cards: Plastic cards coded to open one guest room for the length of a stay. A lost card can be canceled and replaced without changing the lock.
HT-10.Online ordering: A website or app, run by the restaurant or by a delivery company, that takes food orders for pickup or delivery.
HT-10.Self-service kiosk: A touchscreen station where guests check in to a hotel or place and pay for a food order without help from an employee.
HT-10.Contactless payment: Paying by tapping a card or phone on a reader instead of handing over cash or a card, which speeds up checkout.
HT-10.QR code menus: A square code on the table that guests scan with a phone camera to open the menu, and in some restaurants to order and pay.
HT-10.Property management system: The main software of a hotel, often shortened to PMS. It tracks reservations, room status, check-in and check-out, and each guest's bill.
HT-10.Handheld ordering tablets: Portable devices servers carry to enter orders and take payment at the table, sending each order straight to the kitchen.
HT-10.Security cameras: Video cameras that watch entrances, hallways, parking areas and cash registers to deter theft and record incidents.
HT-10.Digital signage: Electronic screens that show menus, prices, event schedules or directions and can be updated instantly from a computer.
HT-10.Table reservation system: Restaurant software that takes bookings, assigns tables, manages the waiting list and tracks how long each party stays.
HT-10.Mobile key: A digital room key sent to a guest's smartphone, so the guest can skip the front desk and unlock the door with the phone.
HT-10.Kitchen display system: Screens in the kitchen that show incoming orders in place of paper tickets and track how long each order has been waiting.
HT-10.Customer relationship management system: A database of guests' contact details, past visits and preferences, often shortened to CRM, used to personalize service and marketing.
HT-10.Central reservation system: Software that holds room availability and rates for every hotel in a chain, so a booking can be made for any of them in one place.
HT-10.Chatbots: Computer programs that answer common guest questions by text or on a website at any hour, such as check-in times or opening hours.
HT-10.Scheduling software: A program managers use to build staff schedules, track hours worked and match the number of workers to expected business.
HT-10.Inventory management software: A program that tracks food, beverage and supply stock, warns when items run low and helps managers order the right amounts.
HT-10.Smart room controls: In-room technology that lets a guest adjust lighting, temperature and entertainment from a tablet, a phone or by voice.
HT-10.Revenue management system: Software that studies demand and booking patterns and recommends the room rate to charge on each date.
HT-10.Channel manager: Software that updates a hotel's rates and room availability on every booking website at once, which helps prevent double bookings.
HT-10.Global distribution system: A worldwide computer network, often shortened to GDS, that travel agents use to see and book hotel rooms, flights and rental cars.
HT-10.Robots: Machines that carry out simple tasks such as delivering items to guest rooms, running food to tables or cleaning floors.
HT-10.Accounting software: A program that records income and expenses, pays suppliers and staff, and produces the financial reports of the business.
HT-10.Guest paging system: Handheld buzzers, or text messages to a phone, that tell waiting guests their table or order is ready.

HT-11.Server: Takes orders and brings food and drinks to the table. In a full-service restaurant most of a server's income usually comes from tips.
HT-11.Bartender: Mixes and serves drinks at a bar. Guests usually tip on each drink or on the total bar tab.
HT-11.Delivery driver: Brings restaurant orders to a customer's home or office. Customers tip in cash at the door or through the ordering app.
HT-11.Valet: Parks and brings back guests' cars at a hotel, restaurant or event. Guests usually tip when the car is returned.
HT-11.Bellhop: Carries a guest's luggage to and from the hotel room and explains the room's features. Guests usually tip for each bag.
HT-11.Housekeeper: Cleans and restocks hotel guest rooms. Guests are encouraged to leave a tip in the room each day, though many forget.
HT-11.Taxi driver: Drives travelers between airports, hotels and attractions for a fare. Passengers usually add a tip in cash or through the app.
HT-11.Barista: Makes and serves coffee drinks. Customers leave tips in a jar at the counter or add one on the payment screen.
HT-11.Tour guide: Leads visitors around a site, city or region and explains what they are seeing. Travelers usually tip at the end of the tour.
HT-11.Busser: Clears and resets tables and refills water. Bussers usually receive a share of the servers' tips, called a tip-out.
HT-11.Concierge: A hotel employee who books restaurants, tickets and tours for guests. Guests tip for special help, such as getting a hard-to-find reservation.
HT-11.Host: Greets diners, manages the waiting list and seats parties. In many restaurants hosts receive a share of the servers' tips.
HT-11.Room service attendant: Delivers meals to hotel guest rooms. A service charge is often added to the bill, and some guests tip on top of it.
HT-11.Shuttle driver: Drives guests between a hotel, the airport and attractions, or drives a tour bus. Passengers often tip, especially for help with bags.
HT-11.Door attendant: Greets guests at a hotel entrance, opens doors, calls taxis and helps with luggage. Guests tip for these small services.
HT-11.Casino dealer: Runs a table game such as blackjack or roulette. Players tip the dealer, and at many casinos the dealers pool and share those tips.
HT-11.Spa therapist: Gives massages, facials or nail treatments at a hotel or resort spa. Guests usually tip a percentage of the treatment price.
HT-11.Food runner: Carries finished dishes from the kitchen to the right table so servers can stay with their guests. Runners usually share in the servers' tips.
HT-11.Banquet server: Serves food and drinks at weddings, meetings and other catered events. Their tips usually come from a service charge added to the event bill.
HT-11.Skycap: An airport porter who checks bags at the curb and helps travelers with luggage. Travelers usually tip for each bag.
HT-11.Cabin steward: Cleans and looks after passengers' cabins on a cruise ship. Cruise lines usually add a daily gratuity to each passenger's account for the crew.
HT-11.Coat check attendant: Stores coats and bags for guests at a restaurant, theater or event. Guests usually tip when they collect their things.
HT-11.Sommelier: A restaurant's wine expert, who helps guests choose and then serves the wine. Sommeliers usually receive a share of the tips.
HT-11.Golf caddie: Carries a golfer's clubs at a golf resort and gives advice on the course. Golfers tip the caddie at the end of the round.
HT-11.Barback: Helps the bartenders by restocking ice, glasses and bottles. Barbacks are paid partly from a share of the bartenders' tips.
HT-11.Pool attendant: Sets up chairs, umbrellas and towels and may bring drinks at a resort pool or beach. Guests tip for the setup and service.
HT-11.Restroom attendant: Keeps a restroom clean and stocked and hands out towels at some upscale restaurants, clubs and hotels, working mostly for tips.
HT-11.Sports instructor: Teaches visitors an activity such as skiing, surfing or scuba diving at a resort. Guests often tip after a lesson.

HT-12.Wheelchair ramps: Sloped surfaces that take the place of steps, so guests who use wheelchairs, walkers or scooters can get into and around the building.
HT-12.Elevators: Machines that carry guests between floors, so people who cannot use stairs can reach rooms and facilities on upper levels.
HT-12.Accessible parking: Wider marked spaces close to the entrance, set aside for vehicles displaying a disability permit.
HT-12.Accessible restrooms: Restrooms with a larger stall, grab bars and a sink and fixtures that a guest in a wheelchair can reach and use.
HT-12.Accessible guest rooms: Hotel rooms built with extra floor space, wider doors and adapted bathrooms for guests with limited mobility, hearing or sight.
HT-12.Grab bars: Sturdy bars fixed to the wall beside toilets and inside showers and tubs, giving guests support as they sit, stand or move across.
HT-12.Braille signage: Signs with raised letters and Braille dots on room numbers, elevator buttons and restroom doors, read by touch by guests who are blind.
HT-12.Wide doorways: Doors and corridors wide enough for a wheelchair or walker to pass through easily.
HT-12.Automatic doors: Doors that open by sensor or push button, so a guest does not have to pull a heavy door by hand.
HT-12.Service animals welcome: Allowing trained service animals, such as guide dogs, to go with their handlers wherever guests may go, even where pets are not allowed.
HT-12.Roll-in showers: Showers with no raised edge, so a wheelchair can roll straight in. They usually have a seat and a handheld shower head.
HT-12.Lowered counters: A section of the front desk, bar or service counter set at a height a guest seated in a wheelchair can reach and use.
HT-12.Accessible tables: Dining tables with enough space underneath and around them for a guest in a wheelchair to pull up and sit comfortably.
HT-12.Staff training: Teaching employees how to serve guests with disabilities respectfully, for example by speaking to the guest directly and offering help without assuming.
HT-12.Braille or large-print menus: Menus and printed information produced in Braille or in oversized type for guests who are blind or have low vision.
HT-12.Visual alarms: Fire alarms and door or phone alerts that flash a bright light, so guests who are deaf or hard of hearing are warned.
HT-12.Closed captioning: Text on a television screen that shows what is being said, so guests who are deaf or hard of hearing can follow a program.
HT-12.Pool lifts: Powered seats, or gently sloped entries, that let a guest with limited mobility get into and out of a swimming pool or hot tub.
HT-12.Accessible website: A website and booking system built to work with screen readers and keyboard navigation, so guests with disabilities can book on their own.
HT-12.Accessible routes: Step-free paths from the parking lot and entrance to guest rooms, dining areas and other facilities.
HT-12.Personal assistance: Help offered by staff on request, such as reading a menu aloud, carrying luggage or guiding a guest to a room or table.
HT-12.Assistive listening devices: Equipment such as hearing loops and amplified telephones that makes sound clearer for guests who are hard of hearing.
HT-12.Text telephones: Devices, often called TTY, that let guests who are deaf or have a speech disability use the telephone by typing messages.
HT-12.Lever door handles: Handles that are pushed down instead of gripped and twisted, which are easier for guests with limited hand strength.
HT-12.Lowered room fixtures: Peepholes, light switches, closet rods and thermostats placed low enough to be used from a wheelchair.
HT-12.Accessible shuttle: A hotel or airport shuttle fitted with a lift or ramp, so guests who use wheelchairs can ride it like any other guest.
HT-12.Sign language interpreters: People who translate between spoken English and sign language, arranged for guests who are deaf at meetings and events.

LDG-10.Sales tax: A state or local tax charged as a percentage of the room rate and of most other purchases the guest makes at the hotel.
LDG-10.Parking fee: A nightly charge for leaving a car in the hotel's lot or garage, or for having a valet park it.
LDG-10.Room service charges: The price of food and drinks delivered to the guest room, usually with a delivery fee and a service charge added.
LDG-10.Resort fee: A mandatory daily charge said to cover facilities such as the pool, fitness center and Wi-Fi. It is added whether or not the guest uses them.
LDG-10.Minibar charges: The price of snacks and drinks the guest takes from the small stocked refrigerator in the room.
LDG-10.Pet fee: A charge for bringing an animal, meant to cover the extra cleaning needed after the stay.
LDG-10.Occupancy tax: A local tax charged on hotel stays, also called a lodging, room or bed tax. Cities often spend the money on tourism promotion.
LDG-10.Wi-Fi fee: A charge for internet access, or for a faster connection, at hotels that do not include it in the room rate.
LDG-10.Late checkout fee: A charge for keeping the room past the normal checkout time, since housekeeping then has less time to prepare it for the next guest.
LDG-10.Restaurant and bar charges: Meals and drinks bought in the hotel's outlets and charged to the room instead of being paid for at the table.
LDG-10.Early check-in fee: A charge for getting into the room before the normal check-in time, when the hotel is able to offer it.
LDG-10.Extra person charge: An added nightly amount when more guests stay in a room than the quoted rate covers, usually beyond two adults.
LDG-10.Smoking fee: A penalty charged when a guest smokes in a non-smoking room, to pay for the deep cleaning needed to remove the smell.
LDG-10.Damage charges: The cost of repairing or replacing hotel property that the guest broke, stained or took, such as furniture, linens or a key card.
LDG-10.Cancellation fee: A charge, often equal to one night's room and tax, when a guest cancels after the deadline or does not arrive at all.
LDG-10.Spa charges: The price of treatments such as massages and facials, billed to the room account.
LDG-10.Laundry charges: A per-item price for having the hotel wash, dry clean or press the guest's clothing.
LDG-10.Service charge: A set percentage added to a bill in place of, or on top of, a voluntary tip. It is common on room service and banquet charges.
LDG-10.Telephone charges: Fees for calls made from the guest room telephone, especially long-distance and international calls.
LDG-10.Pay-per-view movies: A charge for each film or premium program the guest orders on the room television.
LDG-10.Rollaway bed fee: A nightly charge for bringing a portable extra bed, or in some hotels a crib, into the room.
LDG-10.Cleaning fee: An extra charge when a room needs much more cleaning than normal after the guest leaves. Vacation rentals commonly add one to every stay.
LDG-10.Gift shop purchases: Items bought in the hotel's shop or lobby market, such as snacks, toiletries and souvenirs, and charged to the room.
LDG-10.Early departure fee: A charge some hotels apply when a guest checks out before the departure date that was booked, leaving a room unsold.
LDG-10.In-room safe fee: A small daily charge some hotels add for the safe in the room, whether or not the guest uses it.
LDG-10.Energy surcharge: A small daily fee some hotels have added to pass rising electricity and heating costs on to guests.
LDG-10.Package handling fee: A charge for receiving, storing or delivering parcels sent to a guest at the hotel, common at convention hotels.
LDG-10.Business center charges: Fees for printing, copying, faxing or shipping done in the hotel's business center.
LDG-10.Airport shuttle fee: A charge for riding the hotel's van to or from the airport, at hotels where the shuttle is not free.

LDG-11.Security cameras: Video cameras covering entrances, lobbies, hallways and parking areas, which deter crime and record what happened if there is an incident.
LDG-11.Electronic key cards: Room keys coded for one room and one stay. The code changes for each new guest, so an old or lost card stops working.
LDG-11.Security guards: Trained staff who patrol the property, watch for trouble and respond to disturbances and emergencies.
LDG-11.Smoke detectors: Devices in rooms and hallways that sense smoke and sound an alarm, giving guests early warning of a fire.
LDG-11.Fire sprinklers: Ceiling-mounted devices that spray water automatically when they sense the heat of a fire, slowing it before it can spread.
LDG-11.Deadbolts and door latches: Extra locks a guest sets from inside the room, so the door cannot be opened from the hallway even with a key.
LDG-11.In-room safes: Small lockable boxes where guests can secure passports, cash, jewelry and electronics while they are out of the room.
LDG-11.Fire extinguishers: Portable devices placed along hallways and in kitchens that staff or guests can use to put out a small fire.
LDG-11.Emergency exits: Clearly marked doors and stairways that give guests a way out of the building if there is a fire or other emergency.
LDG-11.Peepholes: Small viewers set in guest room doors, so a guest can see who is outside before opening.
LDG-11.Evacuation maps: Diagrams posted on the back of each guest room door showing the nearest exits and the route to reach them.
LDG-11.Good lighting: Bright lighting in parking lots, entrances and corridors, which helps prevent falls and discourages crime.
LDG-11.Restricted building access: Locking side doors, elevators or guest floors so they open only with a valid room key, keeping people who are not guests out.
LDG-11.Verifying identification: Checking a photo ID before issuing or replacing a room key, so a stranger cannot get into someone else's room.
LDG-11.Staff training: Teaching employees what to do in a fire, a medical emergency or a security threat, so they can guide and help guests.
LDG-11.Keeping room numbers private: Writing a guest's room number down instead of saying it aloud, and never telling callers or visitors which room a guest is in.
LDG-11.Emergency plan: Written procedures for fires, severe weather, power failures and other crises, practiced in drills so staff respond quickly.
LDG-11.First aid kits and defibrillators: Medical supplies and automated devices that can shock a heart back into a normal rhythm, kept on site so trained staff can help until an ambulance arrives.
LDG-11.Lifeguards and pool rules: Supervision, depth markers, posted rules and fencing that reduce the risk of drowning and injuries around the swimming pool.
LDG-11.Key control: Strict tracking of master keys and key-making equipment, so keys that open many rooms cannot be lost, copied or misused.
LDG-11.Employee background checks: Screening job applicants before hiring, since many hotel employees are able to enter guest rooms.
LDG-11.Carbon monoxide detectors: Alarms that sense carbon monoxide, a poisonous gas with no smell that can leak from heaters, boilers and other fuel-burning equipment.
LDG-11.Emergency lighting and backup power: Battery-powered lights and generators that keep hallways, stairs and exit signs lit if the electricity fails.
LDG-11.Slip-resistant surfaces: Bath mats, textured flooring and wet floor signs that help prevent slips and falls, one of the most common guest injuries.
LDG-11.Staff uniforms and name badges: Clothing and badges that let guests tell real employees from strangers before opening a door or handing over luggage.

LDG-12.Demand: How many travelers are expected to want a room that night. Rates rise when demand is forecast to be strong and fall when it is weak.
LDG-12.Season: The time of year. Hotels charge more in the peak season, when many people want to visit, and less in the off season.
LDG-12.Competitor rates: What similar hotels nearby are charging for the same night. A hotel compares itself with a chosen group of rivals called its competitive set.
LDG-12.Day of the week: Business hotels are usually busiest midweek and resorts on weekends, so rates differ from one night of the week to the next.
LDG-12.Local events: Conventions, concerts, games and festivals bring a surge of visitors, which lets hotels in the area charge higher rates.
LDG-12.Occupancy: The share of rooms already booked for that night, which shows how many are left to sell. The fuller the hotel is, the more it can charge for the rooms that remain.
LDG-12.Holidays: Public holidays and school vacations change travel patterns, lifting leisure demand and reducing business travel.
LDG-12.Historical data: Records of rates, bookings and occupancy on the same dates in past years, used as the starting point for a forecast.
LDG-12.Room type: The size, bed type, view and features of the room. Suites and rooms with better views are priced above standard rooms.
LDG-12.Costs: What it costs to clean, supply and service an occupied room. A rate must at least cover this cost to be worth accepting.
LDG-12.Booking pace: How quickly reservations for a future date are coming in compared with normal. A fast pace is a sign that rates can go up.
LDG-12.Lead time: How far ahead of arrival guests are booking. Rates are often adjusted as the date gets closer and remaining demand becomes clearer.
LDG-12.Length of stay: How many nights a guest wants. A hotel may discount longer stays, or require a minimum stay over a busy period.
LDG-12.Market segment: The kind of guest who is booking, such as business, leisure or group. Each segment is willing to pay a different price.
LDG-12.Group bookings: Blocks of rooms held for conventions, tours or weddings at a discounted rate, which leave fewer rooms for higher-paying guests.
LDG-12.Distribution channel: Where the booking comes from. A room sold through an online travel agency costs the hotel a commission, while a direct booking does not.
LDG-12.Economic conditions: The health of the wider economy. In a downturn companies and families cut travel, so hotels lower rates to attract them.
LDG-12.Price sensitivity: How strongly guests react to a change in price. Leisure travelers tend to shop around more than business travelers do.
LDG-12.Cancellations and no-shows: The share of bookings expected to cancel or fail to arrive, which affects how many rooms will really be filled.
LDG-12.Weather: The forecast for the dates in question. Good weather lifts last-minute demand at beach and ski resorts, and storms can cut it.
LDG-12.Brand positioning: The quality and price level the hotel wants to be known for. A luxury hotel will not discount so deeply that it harms its image.
LDG-12.Online reviews: The hotel's ratings on review sites. A property with better scores than its rivals can charge more and still win bookings.
LDG-12.Revenue goals: The income targets set in the hotel's budget, which guide how hard the hotel pushes rate compared with occupancy.
LDG-12.New supply: New hotels or rental properties opening nearby, which add rooms to the market and put pressure on every hotel's rates.
LDG-12.Rate parity: An agreement to offer the same rate for the same room on every booking channel, which limits where a hotel can discount.
LDG-12.Total guest spending: What a guest is likely to spend on dining, the spa and other services. A hotel may accept a lower room rate from a guest who spends more overall.

RFS-10.Oven: An enclosed, heated chamber for baking and roasting. Many commercial kitchens use convection ovens, which have a fan that moves the hot air so food cooks faster and more evenly.
RFS-10.Range: A cooking unit with open burners or flat heating surfaces on top, used for pots and pans. At home it is usually called a stove.
RFS-10.Refrigerator: A cooled cabinet that keeps perishable food cold enough to slow the growth of bacteria. A unit with doors you reach into is called a reach-in.
RFS-10.Deep fryer: A tank of hot oil with baskets for cooking foods such as french fries and fried chicken quickly and evenly.
RFS-10.Grill: A cooking surface of metal bars over a gas, electric or charcoal heat source, which gives food grill marks and a charred flavor.
RFS-10.Dishwasher: A machine that washes, rinses and sanitizes dishes, glasses and utensils far faster than washing them by hand.
RFS-10.Freezer: A cabinet or room that keeps food frozen solid for long-term storage, from small reach-in units to large walk-in rooms.
RFS-10.Smallwares: The trade name for hand tools and cookware such as pots, pans, knives, tongs, ladles and cutting boards.
RFS-10.Griddle: A flat, solid metal cooking surface, also called a flat top, used for foods such as pancakes, eggs and burgers.
RFS-10.Walk-in cooler: A refrigerated room big enough to step inside, used to store large amounts of cold food on shelves.
RFS-10.Mixer: A machine with a bowl and rotating attachments that mixes batters, kneads dough and whips cream in large batches.
RFS-10.Microwave: An oven that heats food quickly with microwave energy, used in commercial kitchens mostly for reheating and thawing.
RFS-10.Sink: Kitchens have separate sinks for separate jobs: a three-compartment sink to wash, rinse and sanitize pots by hand, a prep sink for food and a sink used only for washing hands.
RFS-10.Meat slicer: A machine with a spinning circular blade that cuts meat, cheese and other foods into even slices of a set thickness.
RFS-10.Food processor: A machine with fast-spinning blades or discs that chops, slices, shreds and purees food in seconds.
RFS-10.Blender: A machine with blades at the bottom of a tall container, or on a handheld stick, used to puree soups, sauces and drinks.
RFS-10.Hot-holding equipment: Steam tables, heat lamps and warming cabinets that keep cooked food at a safe hot temperature until it is served. A steam table is a heated counter that holds pans of food.
RFS-10.Prep table: A stainless steel work surface where cooks cut, mix and assemble food. Some have refrigerated storage built in underneath.
RFS-10.Exhaust hood: A ventilation canopy above the cooking line that draws heat, smoke and grease-filled air out of the kitchen.
RFS-10.Ice machine: A machine that makes and stores ice for drinks and for keeping food cold.
RFS-10.Steamer: A sealed cabinet that cooks vegetables, rice, seafood and other foods with steam, which keeps in moisture and nutrients.
RFS-10.Shelving: Racks, usually of metal wire, that keep stored food and supplies organized and up off the floor.
RFS-10.Toaster: A machine that browns bread and buns. High-volume kitchens use conveyor models that toast continuously.
RFS-10.Steam-jacketed kettle: A large pot with hollow walls heated by steam, used to cook soups, stocks and sauces in big batches without scorching.
RFS-10.Tilting skillet: A large, flat-bottomed pan on a frame that can braise, fry, simmer or griddle food and then tilts to pour it out.
RFS-10.Combi oven: An oven that cooks with dry heat, steam or a mix of both, so one unit can roast, bake and steam.
RFS-10.Proofer: A warm, humid cabinet that helps yeast dough rise before it is baked.
RFS-10.Blast chiller: A unit that cools hot food very quickly with fast-moving cold air, bringing it down through the unsafe temperature range before bacteria can multiply.
RFS-10.Salamander: A small, very hot overhead broiler used to brown, glaze or melt the top of a dish just before it is served.

RFS-11.Baking: Cooking food with dry, hot air in an oven. The term is used mostly for breads, pastries, cakes and casseroles.
RFS-11.Grilling: Cooking food on a grate above a heat source, which gives it char marks and a smoky flavor.
RFS-11.Deep-frying: Cooking food completely covered in hot oil or fat, which gives it a crisp, golden outside.
RFS-11.Boiling: Cooking food in liquid that is bubbling rapidly at its boiling point, as is done with pasta and potatoes.
RFS-11.Roasting: Cooking food uncovered in an oven with dry heat. The term is used mostly for meats, poultry and vegetables.
RFS-11.Sauteing: Cooking small or thin pieces of food quickly in a little fat in a hot pan, tossing or stirring as they cook.
RFS-11.Steaming: Cooking food in the vapor above boiling water, without letting it touch the water. It keeps color, texture and nutrients well.
RFS-11.Broiling: Cooking food with strong direct heat from above, the reverse of grilling, where the heat comes from below.
RFS-11.Simmering: Cooking food gently in liquid kept just below the boiling point, with only small bubbles rising to the surface.
RFS-11.Stir-frying: Cooking bite-sized pieces very quickly in a little oil over high heat while stirring constantly, traditionally in a wok.
RFS-11.Barbecuing: Cooking meat slowly at a low temperature with wood smoke or over coals, often with a seasoning rub or sauce.
RFS-11.Poaching: Cooking delicate foods such as eggs or fish gently in liquid that is hot but not bubbling.
RFS-11.Braising: Browning a large piece of food, then cooking it slowly in a covered pot with a small amount of liquid until tender.
RFS-11.Stewing: Cooking small pieces of food slowly while fully covered in liquid, which becomes part of the finished dish.
RFS-11.Smoking: Cooking or flavoring food with the smoke from burning or smoldering wood, usually over a long time at low heat.
RFS-11.Searing: Browning the surface of food quickly over very high heat to build flavor and color, usually before finishing it another way.
RFS-11.Pan-frying: Cooking food in a pan with a moderate amount of fat, more than for sauteing but not enough to cover the food.
RFS-11.Blanching: Cooking food very briefly in boiling water, then usually cooling it at once in ice water to stop the cooking.
RFS-11.Microwaving: Heating food with microwave energy, which makes the water in the food heat up. It is fast but does not brown food.
RFS-11.Sous vide: Sealing food in an airtight bag and cooking it in a water bath held at an exact, fairly low temperature. The name is French for under vacuum.
RFS-11.Pressure cooking: Cooking food in a sealed pot where trapped steam raises the pressure and temperature, so the food cooks much faster.
RFS-11.Slow cooking: Cooking food for many hours at a low temperature, usually in a covered pot with liquid, to make it tender.
RFS-11.Air frying: Cooking food with very hot air moved rapidly by a fan, which gives a crisp surface with little or no oil.
RFS-11.Griddling: Cooking food on a flat, solid, heated metal surface, as is done with pancakes, eggs and smash burgers.
RFS-11.Confit: Cooking food slowly while it is covered in fat at a low temperature. Duck legs cooked in duck fat are the classic example.
RFS-11.En papillote: Baking food sealed inside a folded parcel of parchment paper, so it steams in its own juices. The name is French.
RFS-11.Sweating: Cooking vegetables gently in a little fat over low heat so they soften and release moisture without browning.

RFS-12.Target customers: The people the restaurant wants to attract. Their ages, incomes, tastes and reasons for dining out shape which dishes will sell.
RFS-12.Food cost: What the ingredients for a dish cost. An item belongs on the menu only if it can be sold at a price that covers this cost and leaves a profit.
RFS-12.Menu prices: What guests will be asked to pay. Each item's price has to fit both the restaurant's price range and what its customers are willing to spend.
RFS-12.Profitability: How much money each item contributes after its costs. Planners favor dishes that are both popular and profitable.
RFS-12.Ingredient availability: Whether suppliers can deliver an ingredient reliably, in the quantity and quality needed, all the time the item is on the menu.
RFS-12.Seasonality: The time of year. Produce is cheaper and better in season, and guests want lighter dishes in summer and heartier ones in winter.
RFS-12.Kitchen equipment: The equipment and space the kitchen has. A menu full of fried foods will not work in a kitchen with a single fryer.
RFS-12.Staff skills: What the cooks and servers are able to prepare and serve well. Complicated dishes need trained staff and cost more in labor.
RFS-12.Restaurant concept: The theme, cuisine and style of the restaurant. Every item should fit the concept so the menu feels consistent to guests.
RFS-12.Dietary needs: Guests' needs and choices, such as vegetarian, vegan, gluten-free or religious diets, which a balanced menu makes room for.
RFS-12.Allergens: Ingredients such as peanuts, milk and shellfish that can cause dangerous reactions. Planners decide how to limit, label or separate them.
RFS-12.Nutrition: The health value of the dishes. Many guests look for lighter choices, and some food service operations must meet nutrition standards.
RFS-12.Variety and balance: A mix of flavors, colors, textures, cooking methods and main ingredients, so guests have real choices and the menu is not repetitive.
RFS-12.Competition: What nearby restaurants offer and charge. A menu should give guests a reason to choose this restaurant over its rivals.
RFS-12.Food trends: Dishes, ingredients and eating habits that are growing in popularity, which a restaurant may add to stay current.
RFS-12.Preparation time: How long a dish takes to prepare and cook. Items that are slow to make hold up the kitchen during a rush.
RFS-12.Item popularity: How well each dish has sold in the past. Sales records show which items to keep, promote or remove.
RFS-12.Local tastes: The food preferences and customs of the region and community the restaurant serves.
RFS-12.Storage space: How much refrigerator, freezer and dry storage the restaurant has, which limits how many different ingredients it can stock.
RFS-12.Meal period: The part of the day being served, such as breakfast, lunch or dinner. Each one calls for different foods, prices and speed.
RFS-12.Menu size: The number of items offered. A long menu gives choice but adds inventory, waste and work, and a short one is easier to do well.
RFS-12.Presentation: How a dish will look on the plate. Color, height and arrangement affect how appealing guests find it.
RFS-12.Portion size: How much food is served in each order, which affects the cost of the dish, its price and how satisfied the guest feels.
RFS-12.Cross-utilization: Planning dishes that share ingredients, so each ingredient is used in several items and less of it spoils.
RFS-12.Truth in menu: The requirement that menu descriptions be accurate. Claims about size, origin, freshness or preparation must match what is served.
RFS-12.Station workload: How orders will be spread across kitchen stations. If too many dishes come from the grill, that one station falls behind.
RFS-12.Service style: How the food will reach the guest. Dishes for takeout or delivery must hold up during travel, and buffet items must hold well on a line.
RFS-12.Waste and spoilage: How quickly ingredients go bad and how much is trimmed away. Highly perishable items are risky unless they sell steadily.
RFS-12.Food safety risk: How risky an item is to handle safely. Raw or undercooked foods, such as oysters or rare burgers, need extra controls.

RFS-13.Salmonella: Bacteria that live in the intestines of people and animals and are most often linked to raw poultry, eggs and contaminated produce.
RFS-13.E. coli: Bacteria that live in the intestines of people and animals. Most strains are harmless, but some make a toxin and are linked to undercooked ground beef and contaminated produce.
RFS-13.Norovirus: A highly contagious virus that causes vomiting and diarrhea. It is often spread when an infected food handler touches ready-to-eat food.
RFS-13.Listeria: Bacteria that can keep growing at refrigerator temperatures. They are linked to deli meats, soft cheeses and unpasteurized milk, and are a serious risk in pregnancy.
RFS-13.Hepatitis A: A virus that infects the liver. It spreads when an infected food handler does not wash hands properly, and through shellfish from contaminated water.
RFS-13.Clostridium botulinum: Bacteria that grow where there is no oxygen, such as in improperly canned food, and make the toxin that causes botulism, a rare but very dangerous illness.
RFS-13.Staphylococcus aureus: Bacteria carried on many people's skin and in their noses. Food handlers can transfer them to food, where they can make a toxin that normal cooking does not destroy.
RFS-13.Mold: A type of fungus that grows on food. Some molds produce toxins, such as aflatoxin on grains and nuts, that can make people ill.
RFS-13.Campylobacter: Bacteria most often linked to raw or undercooked poultry and to unpasteurized milk.
RFS-13.Shigella: Bacteria carried in human waste. They spread when food handlers do not wash their hands after using the restroom, and through contaminated water.
RFS-13.Trichinella: A parasitic roundworm that people can get from eating undercooked pork or wild game, causing an illness called trichinosis.
RFS-13.Clostridium perfringens: Bacteria that multiply in cooked meats, stews and gravies that are cooled too slowly or held at unsafe temperatures.
RFS-13.Bacillus cereus: Bacteria whose spores survive cooking. They are linked to cooked rice and other starchy foods left too long at room temperature.
RFS-13.Vibrio: Bacteria that live in warm coastal waters. They are linked to raw or undercooked oysters and other shellfish.
RFS-13.Giardia: A parasite found in contaminated water, which can reach food through that water or through an infected food handler.
RFS-13.Mushroom toxins: Natural poisons in some wild mushrooms, which cooking and freezing do not destroy. This is why kitchens buy mushrooms only from approved suppliers.
RFS-13.Tapeworm: A parasitic flatworm that people can get from eating raw or undercooked beef, pork or fish that carries its larvae.
RFS-13.Anisakis: A parasitic worm found in some raw or undercooked fish, such as herring, cod and salmon. Proper freezing or cooking kills it.
RFS-13.Cryptosporidium: A parasite found in contaminated water and on produce washed or watered with it. It can also be spread by infected food handlers.
RFS-13.Cyclospora: A parasite linked to fresh produce, such as berries, herbs and lettuce, that has been contaminated by unclean water.
RFS-13.Toxoplasma: A parasite that people can get from undercooked meat or from food contaminated by cat waste. It is a particular risk during pregnancy.
RFS-13.Histamine: A toxin that builds up in fish such as tuna, mackerel and mahi-mahi when they are not kept cold. Cooking does not destroy it.
RFS-13.Ciguatoxin: A toxin found in some large reef fish, such as barracuda and grouper, that have eaten smaller fish carrying it. Cooking does not destroy it.
RFS-13.Shellfish toxins: Toxins made by certain algae that build up in clams, mussels, oysters and scallops. Cooking and freezing do not destroy them.
RFS-13.Yersinia: Bacteria linked mainly to raw or undercooked pork. Like Listeria, they are able to grow at refrigerator temperatures.

TRV-09.Flights: Air travel to and from the destination. It is often the most expensive single part of a package.
TRV-09.Hotel accommodations: The room the traveler stays in each night. Together with transportation, lodging is the core of most packages.
TRV-09.Meals: Some or all of the traveler's food. A package may cover only breakfast, or every meal at an all-inclusive resort.
TRV-09.Airport transfers: Transportation between the airport and the hotel, by shuttle, bus or private car, arranged ahead of time by the packager.
TRV-09.Rental car: The use of a rented vehicle for the trip. Packages that combine a flight with a car are known as fly-drive packages.
TRV-09.Guided tours: Organized sightseeing trips led by a guide, such as a city tour or a day trip to a nearby attraction.
TRV-09.Attraction tickets: Prepaid admission to places such as theme parks, museums, shows or ski areas, so the traveler does not pay at the gate.
TRV-09.Activities: Recreation built into the price, such as snorkeling, golf, a cooking class or a spa treatment.
TRV-09.Tour guide: A professional who travels with the group or meets it locally, to explain the sights and handle the day-to-day arrangements.
TRV-09.Cruise: Passage and a cabin on a cruise ship. The cruise fare already bundles lodging, most meals and onboard entertainment.
TRV-09.Drinks: Beverages, sometimes including alcohol, covered by the package price instead of being paid for one at a time.
TRV-09.Travel insurance: Coverage that repays the traveler for losses such as a canceled trip, lost luggage or a medical emergency away from home.
TRV-09.Entertainment: Shows, concerts or evening events whose tickets are part of the package price.
TRV-09.Taxes and fees: Government taxes, airport and port charges and resort fees that the packager collects up front as part of one price.
TRV-09.Gratuities: Tips for guides, drivers, servers and housekeepers, paid in advance so the traveler does not need to tip during the trip.
TRV-09.Baggage handling: Having luggage carried between the airport, the tour bus and the hotel room, a common feature of escorted tours.
TRV-09.Rail or motorcoach travel: Tickets for travel by train, bus or ferry between the places visited on the trip.
TRV-09.Equipment rental: The use of gear the trip requires, such as skis, snorkeling equipment, bicycles or golf clubs.
TRV-09.Resort credits: A set dollar amount the traveler can spend at the resort or on the ship, for example on dining or the spa, added to make a package more attractive.
TRV-09.Childcare: Supervised children's clubs or babysitting, which family resorts and cruise lines often build into their packages.
TRV-09.Welcome reception: A group meal or party at the start, or sometimes the end, of a tour, where travelers meet the guide and one another.
TRV-09.Visa assistance: Help with applying for, or paying for, the entry documents the destination country requires.
TRV-09.Wi-Fi: Internet access at the hotel or on the ship, covered by the package instead of being charged for separately.
TRV-09.Traveler assistance: Access to a local representative or an emergency phone line who can help if something goes wrong during the trip.

TRV-10.Security checkpoint: The screening point where passengers and their carry-on bags are checked for prohibited items before entering the gate area.
TRV-10.Check-in counters: Airline desks where passengers confirm they are flying, hand over checked bags and collect boarding passes.
TRV-10.Baggage claim: The hall where arriving passengers collect checked luggage from moving belts called carousels.
TRV-10.Gates: The numbered waiting areas where passengers gather to board, each one leading to a parked aircraft.
TRV-10.Restaurants: Food courts, cafes, bars and sit-down restaurants that serve passengers waiting for flights and pay the airport rent or a share of sales.
TRV-10.Shops: Stores selling travel needs, reading material, gifts and luxury goods to passengers who have time to fill before a flight.
TRV-10.Restrooms: Public toilets and washrooms throughout the terminal. Their cleanliness is one of the things passengers rate airports on.
TRV-10.Parking: Lots and garages where travelers leave cars for hours or days. Parking fees are an important source of income for many airports.
TRV-10.Airport lounges: Quiet, comfortable rooms with food, drinks and workspace, open to premium passengers, members and those who pay an entry fee.
TRV-10.Car rental desks: Counters where arriving travelers pick up vehicles they have rented, often grouped together in one rental car center.
TRV-10.Customs and immigration: Government checkpoints where international travelers show passports and declare goods when entering a country.
TRV-10.Duty-free shops: Stores that sell goods such as perfume, alcohol and chocolate to international travelers without certain local taxes.
TRV-10.Ground transportation: Taxis, ride-hailing pickups, buses, hotel shuttles and trains that carry passengers between the airport and the city.
TRV-10.Self-service kiosks: Touchscreen machines where passengers check in, choose seats and print boarding passes and bag tags without an agent.
TRV-10.Information desk: A staffed counter where travelers ask for directions and help with the airport's services or with a flight problem.
TRV-10.Flight information displays: Screens that list departing and arriving flights with their times, gates and status, such as on time or delayed.
TRV-10.Currency exchange and ATMs: Counters and cash machines where international travelers swap one country's money for another's or withdraw local cash.
TRV-10.Wi-Fi and charging stations: Wireless internet and power outlets that let passengers use and recharge phones and laptops while they wait.
TRV-10.Curbside check-in: A service outside the terminal doors where porters called skycaps check passengers' bags as soon as they arrive.
TRV-10.Terminal trains and shuttles: Automated trains, buses and moving walkways that carry passengers between terminals, concourses and parking areas.
TRV-10.Luggage carts: Wheeled carts that passengers use to push heavy bags through the terminal, free at some airports and rented at others.
TRV-10.Lost and found: Offices where passengers report missing or delayed baggage and reclaim items left in the terminal or on an aircraft.
TRV-10.Wheelchair assistance: Staff and equipment that help passengers with limited mobility get through check-in and security and on to the aircraft.
TRV-10.Jet bridges: Enclosed, movable walkways that connect the gate to the aircraft door, so passengers board without going outside.
TRV-10.Airport hotel: A hotel inside or connected to the terminal, used by travelers with early flights, long layovers or canceled connections.
TRV-10.Chapel: A quiet room, usually open to people of all faiths, set aside for prayer and reflection.
TRV-10.Pet relief areas: Marked spaces where service animals and traveling pets can relieve themselves, often located past security.
TRV-10.Nursing rooms: Private rooms or pods where parents can feed and care for babies, part of an airport's services for families.
TRV-10.Medical clinic: A first aid station, clinic or pharmacy that treats passengers and staff who fall ill or are injured at the airport.

TRV-11.Trip cancellation: Repays prepaid, non-refundable trip costs when the traveler has to cancel before leaving for a reason the policy names, such as serious illness.
TRV-11.Lost luggage: Pays for bags and their contents that are lost, stolen or damaged during the trip, up to the limit stated in the policy. For a theft, insurers usually ask for a police report.
TRV-11.Medical emergency: Pays for doctor and hospital care if the traveler becomes ill or is injured during the trip. Health plans from home often give little coverage abroad.
TRV-11.Flight delay or cancellation: Repays extra costs, such as meals and a hotel room, when a covered delay or canceled flight leaves the traveler stranded for a set number of hours.
TRV-11.Trip interruption: Repays the unused part of a trip, and the extra cost of getting home, when the traveler must cut the trip short for a covered reason.
TRV-11.Baggage delay: Pays for essentials such as clothing and toiletries when checked bags arrive many hours later than the traveler does.
TRV-11.Missed connection: Covers the cost of catching up with a trip when a delay causes the traveler to miss a connecting flight or a cruise departure.
TRV-11.Emergency medical evacuation: Pays to transport a seriously ill or injured traveler to the nearest suitable hospital, or home, which can be very expensive.
TRV-11.Rental car damage: Pays for collision damage to, or theft of, a rental vehicle. It is usually sold as an optional extra on a travel policy.
TRV-11.Natural disasters: Covers losses when a hurricane, earthquake or similar event forces a trip to be canceled or cut short, if the policy was bought before the event was known.
TRV-11.Death or illness of a family member: A common covered reason for canceling or interrupting a trip: a close relative dies or becomes seriously ill.
TRV-11.Accidental death: Pays a set sum to the traveler's family if the traveler dies or suffers a severe injury, such as losing a limb, in an accident during the trip.
TRV-11.Supplier bankruptcy: Repays the traveler when an airline, cruise line or tour operator goes out of business and cannot provide what was paid for.
TRV-11.Emergency dental care: Pays for urgent treatment of a dental injury or sudden tooth pain during the trip, up to a small stated limit.
TRV-11.Cancel for any reason: An optional upgrade that repays part of the trip cost even when the reason for canceling is not one the standard policy names.
TRV-11.Terrorism: Many policies cover canceling or interrupting a trip when a terrorist attack happens in a city on the itinerary shortly before or during the visit.
TRV-11.Lost passport: Pays the fees and extra travel costs of replacing a passport or other travel documents lost or stolen during the trip.
TRV-11.Job loss: Some policies repay trip costs if the traveler is laid off through no fault of their own after buying the policy.
TRV-11.Jury duty: Being called to serve on a jury or appear in court on the travel dates is a covered reason for canceling under many policies.
TRV-11.Repatriation of remains: Pays the cost of returning a traveler's body home if the traveler dies during the trip.
TRV-11.Non-medical evacuation: Pays to move the traveler out of a place that has become unsafe because of political unrest or a natural disaster.
TRV-11.Strike: A labor strike that shuts down an airline or other carrier is a covered reason for delay or cancellation under many policies.

TRV-12.Guided tour: A tour led by a guide who shows visitors the sights and explains their history and meaning, such as a city sightseeing tour.
TRV-12.Bus tour: A sightseeing trip by motorcoach. It ranges from a hop-on hop-off city loop to a tour of several days across a region.
TRV-12.Walking tour: A tour on foot through a neighborhood or historic district, led by a guide and usually lasting an hour or two.
TRV-12.Group tour: A tour sold to many travelers who share the same itinerary, transportation and guide, which keeps the price per person down.
TRV-12.Package tour: A trip sold at one price that bundles transportation, lodging and often meals and sightseeing, arranged in advance by a tour operator.
TRV-12.Day trip: A short outing from a base city to a nearby attraction, returning the same day. It is also called an excursion.
TRV-12.Boat tour: A sightseeing trip on the water, such as a harbor cruise, a river cruise or a dinner cruise.
TRV-12.Food tour: A guided visit to several restaurants, markets, wineries or breweries, with tastings along the way.
TRV-12.Private tour: A tour arranged for one traveler, family or small party, with its own guide and an itinerary shaped to their wishes.
TRV-12.Self-guided tour: A tour that travelers follow on their own at their own pace, using a map, an app or a recorded audio guide in place of a live guide.
TRV-12.Escorted tour: A tour on which a professional tour director travels with the group for the whole trip and handles all the arrangements.
TRV-12.Adventure tour: A tour built around physical activity and the outdoors, such as hiking, rafting, kayaking or trekking.
TRV-12.Bike tour: A guided or supported trip by bicycle, lasting from a few hours in a city to several days through the countryside.
TRV-12.Nature and wildlife tour: A trip to see animals and natural scenery in the wild, such as an African safari, a whale-watching cruise or an ecotour of a rainforest.
TRV-12.Historical tour: A tour focused on the past and culture of a place, visiting landmarks, museums, battlefields or historic districts.
TRV-12.Independent tour: A package of flights and hotels for travelers who go on their own without a guide or group. It is known in the trade as FIT.
TRV-12.Shore excursion: A tour sold to cruise passengers for the hours their ship is docked in a port of call.
TRV-12.Air tour: A sightseeing flight by helicopter, small plane or balloon over a landmark or landscape, such as a canyon, volcano or city skyline. The trade calls it flightseeing.
TRV-12.Special-interest tour: A tour planned around a shared hobby or theme, such as gardens, wine, photography, music or sports.
TRV-12.Educational tour: A trip designed for learning, such as a student tour of a capital city or a study tour led by an expert.
TRV-12.Rail tour: A tour that travels mainly by train, often along a scenic route, with sightseeing stops on the way.
TRV-12.Hosted tour: A tour on which travelers move about independently, and a local host at each destination is available to help and give advice.
TRV-12.Incentive tour: A trip that a company buys as a reward for employees or dealers who reach a sales or performance goal.
TRV-12.Familiarization tour: A free or low-cost trip offered to travel agents and writers so that they get to know a destination and recommend it. Often called a fam trip.
TRV-12.Fly-drive tour: A package that combines a flight with a rental car, and often prebooked hotels, so travelers can drive a route on their own.
TRV-12.Step-on guide tour: A tour on which a local expert boards a visiting group's motorcoach and guides it around a city or site.
TRV-12.Virtual tour: A tour delivered online by live or recorded video, letting people see a place without traveling to it.
TRV-12.Pilgrimage: A tour to a place that is sacred to the travelers' faith, organized for religious groups.

TRV-13.Job creation: A positive effect. Hotels, restaurants, attractions and transportation companies hire local people to serve visitors.
TRV-13.Income for local businesses: A positive effect. Money that visitors spend on lodging, food, shopping and activities becomes sales for local firms.
TRV-13.Overcrowding: A negative effect. So many visitors arrive that streets, beaches and attractions are packed, spoiling the place for residents and tourists alike.
TRV-13.Pollution: A negative effect. More visitors mean more litter, sewage, noise and vehicle and aircraft emissions.
TRV-13.Traffic congestion: A negative effect. Visitors' cars, rental vehicles and tour buses clog local roads and fill parking spaces.
TRV-13.Tax revenue: A positive effect. Governments collect lodging, sales and other taxes on visitor spending and can use the money for public services.
TRV-13.Environmental damage: A negative effect. Building resorts and heavy visitor use can destroy habitats, wear away trails and beaches and harm wildlife.
TRV-13.Higher prices: A negative effect. Strong visitor demand pushes up the price of goods, services and land, raising the cost of living for residents.
TRV-13.Improved infrastructure: A positive effect. Roads, airports, utilities and public transportation built or upgraded for visitors also serve residents.
TRV-13.Cultural exchange: A positive effect. Visitors and hosts meet and learn about each other's customs, which can build understanding between cultures.
TRV-13.Rising housing costs: A negative effect. Homes turned into vacation rentals and second homes leave fewer places for residents, so rents and prices climb.
TRV-13.Preservation of heritage: A positive effect. Visitor interest and spending give a community reasons and money to protect historic sites, crafts and traditions.
TRV-13.Loss of local culture: A negative effect. Traditions may be changed or staged to please tourists, and local ways of life can fade or lose their meaning.
TRV-13.Seasonal unemployment: A negative effect. Many tourism jobs last only for the busy season, leaving workers without income for the rest of the year.
TRV-13.Strain on resources: A negative effect. Visitors use large amounts of water, energy and public services, which can leave too little for residents.
TRV-13.Funding for conservation: A positive effect. Park fees and visitor spending can pay to protect wildlife and natural areas, and give them economic value.
TRV-13.Overdependence on tourism: A negative effect. An economy that relies mostly on visitors is hit hard when a recession, disaster or disease outbreak keeps them away.
TRV-13.Crime: A negative effect. Crowds of visitors carrying cash and valuables can attract theft, scams and other crime.
TRV-13.Low-wage jobs: A negative effect. Many of the jobs tourism creates are entry-level service positions with low pay and few benefits.
TRV-13.Community pride: A positive effect. Seeing that visitors value their home can make residents prouder of its culture, history and scenery.
TRV-13.Overdevelopment: A negative effect. Too much building of hotels and attractions uses up open land and can spoil the scenery that drew visitors.
TRV-13.New amenities for residents: A positive effect. Restaurants, shops, parks and entertainment that open to serve visitors are there for local people too.
TRV-13.Foreign exchange earnings: A positive effect. Spending by international visitors brings foreign currency into the country, much as an export does.
TRV-13.Economic leakage: A negative effect. Part of what tourists spend leaves the local economy, to pay for imported goods or as profit for outside owners.
TRV-13.Multiplier effect: A positive effect. Tourist money is spent again by the businesses and workers who receive it, creating more income than the original amount.
TRV-13.Resident displacement: A negative effect. Local people are pushed out of their neighborhoods as land and housing are taken over for tourism.
TRV-13.Resident resentment: A negative effect. Residents grow hostile toward visitors when they feel tourism has made daily life worse.
TRV-13.Diversified economy: A positive effect. Tourism gives a region another source of income, so it depends less on a single industry such as farming or mining.

EVT-09.Ticket sales: Money paid by the public for admission. For concerts, festivals and sporting events it is usually the main source of income.
EVT-09.Sponsorships: Payments from companies in return for exposure to the audience, such as their logo on signs or their name on a stage.
EVT-09.Registration fees: What attendees pay to take part in a conference, convention, race or tournament, usually collected in advance.
EVT-09.Food and beverage sales: Income from meals, snacks and drinks sold at the event by the organizer, or a share of what a caterer sells.
EVT-09.Merchandise sales: Income from selling event-branded items such as T-shirts, programs and souvenirs.
EVT-09.Donations: Gifts of money from individuals or businesses who expect nothing in return. They are central to charity events.
EVT-09.Exhibitor fees: What companies pay to rent booth space on a trade show floor so they can meet attendees and show their products.
EVT-09.Vendor fees: A flat fee or a percentage of sales paid by food trucks, craft sellers and other vendors for the right to sell at the event.
EVT-09.Advertising sales: Income from selling ad space in the printed program, on the event website or app, or on banners at the venue.
EVT-09.Grants: Money awarded by a government agency, tourism office or foundation to support an event that benefits the community. It is not repaid.
EVT-09.Host organization budget: Money the company or association holding the event sets aside to pay for it, common for meetings that charge no admission.
EVT-09.Auctions: Sales of donated items or experiences to the highest bidder, a common way for charity galas to raise money.
EVT-09.Raffles: Sales of numbered tickets for a chance to win a prize. Many places regulate raffles and limit who may hold them.
EVT-09.Parking fees: Charges for parking at the venue, which the organizer keeps or shares with the venue owner.
EVT-09.VIP packages: Higher-priced tickets that add extras such as better seats, a private lounge or a chance to meet a performer.
EVT-09.In-kind sponsorship: Goods or services given by a company instead of cash, such as free printing or drinks, which lower what the event must spend.
EVT-09.Membership dues: Fees members pay to an association, part of which helps pay for the association's annual meeting and other events.
EVT-09.Crowdfunding: Raising many small contributions online from supporters before the event takes place.
EVT-09.Broadcast rights: Fees a television network or streaming service pays for the right to show the event to its audience.
EVT-09.Photo and video sales: Income from selling event photographs, such as race finish photos, or recordings of conference sessions.
EVT-09.Add-on sessions: Extra workshops, tours or social activities that attendees can choose to buy on top of basic registration.
EVT-09.Hotel commissions: A payment or rebate from hotels to the organizer for each room night that attendees book in the event's room block.

EVT-10.Social media: Posts, event pages and paid ads on platforms such as Instagram, Facebook and TikTok, which people can share with their friends.
EVT-10.Email invitations: Messages sent to a list of past attendees, members or customers, announcing the event and linking to registration or tickets.
EVT-10.Flyers and posters: Printed notices handed out or displayed where the target audience will see them, such as schools, shops and community boards.
EVT-10.Event website: A page with the date, place, program and a way to register or buy tickets. Most other promotion sends people here.
EVT-10.Word of mouth: People telling friends, family and coworkers about the event. It costs nothing and is trusted more than advertising.
EVT-10.Paid advertising: Space or time bought in media such as radio, newspapers, billboards or websites to announce the event to a wide audience.
EVT-10.Printed invitations: Cards mailed or handed to chosen guests, often after an earlier save-the-date notice. They are common for weddings and galas.
EVT-10.Press release: A written announcement sent to news outlets in the hope that they will report on the event, which is free publicity.
EVT-10.Early-bird discounts: Lower prices for people who register or buy tickets before a deadline, which brings in early sales and builds momentum.
EVT-10.Influencers: People with a large online following who are paid or invited to tell their audience about the event.
EVT-10.Online event listings: Entries on ticketing sites and community calendars where people look for things to do in their area.
EVT-10.Promotional videos: Short clips, such as a teaser or highlights from last year, that show people what the event will feel like.
EVT-10.Sponsor and partner promotion: Asking sponsors, exhibitors and community partners to announce the event to their own customers and followers.
EVT-10.Contests and giveaways: Offering free tickets or prizes to people who enter, share or sign up, which spreads awareness of the event.
EVT-10.Event hashtag: A short tag used on every social media post about the event, so the posts are easy to find and attendees help spread the word.
EVT-10.Speaker and performer promotion: Announcing well-known speakers or acts, and asking them to tell their own fans and followers that they will appear.
EVT-10.Text messages: Short messages sent to the phones of people who have agreed to receive them, useful for reminders and last-minute offers.
EVT-10.Search engine marketing: Paying for ads on search results, and wording the event page well, so the event appears when people search for related terms.
EVT-10.Referral incentives: Rewards, such as a discount, for attendees who persuade friends or colleagues to register too.
EVT-10.Public announcements: Spoken notices made over a public address system or at meetings, classes and other events where likely attendees are gathered.
EVT-10.Street teams: Groups of staff or volunteers who promote the event face to face in public places, handing out flyers and talking to people who pass.
EVT-10.Media partnerships: Deals in which a radio station, newspaper or other outlet promotes the event in return for being named as a sponsor.
EVT-10.Retargeting ads: Online ads shown to people who visited the event website but left without registering, to remind them to come back.
EVT-10.Personal outreach: Direct phone calls or individual messages to key guests, past attendees or group leaders, inviting them personally.

EVT-11.Budget: A table of every expected cost and source of income for the event, compared with actual figures as money is spent and received.
EVT-11.Contract: A signed, legally binding agreement with a venue, vendor or client that sets out what each side will provide and pay.
EVT-11.Guest list: The record of who is invited or registered, with contact details and replies, used to plan seating, catering and check-in.
EVT-11.Timeline: A dated schedule of every planning task, working backward from the event date, that shows what must be done by when.
EVT-11.Checklist: A list of tasks and items to check off, so that nothing is forgotten during planning or on the day.
EVT-11.Agenda: The order of sessions and activities with their times, given to attendees so they know what happens when.
EVT-11.Floor plan: A scale drawing of the room or site showing where the stage, tables, chairs, exits and equipment will be placed.
EVT-11.Seating chart: A plan that assigns each guest to a table or seat, used for weddings, banquets and other formal dinners.
EVT-11.Invitation: The printed or electronic notice asking people to attend, giving the date, time, place and how to reply.
EVT-11.Invoice: A bill from a vendor or venue listing what was supplied and the amount owed. The planner checks it against the contract before paying.
EVT-11.Menu: The list of food and drinks agreed with the caterer, including any choices for guests with special diets.
EVT-11.Vendor contact list: A sheet of names and phone numbers for every supplier and key person, so that problems on the day can be solved quickly.
EVT-11.Event proposal: A document presenting the planner's concept, program and estimated cost to a client for approval before detailed planning begins.
EVT-11.Run of show: A minute-by-minute schedule for the event day that shows what happens, who is responsible and each technical cue.
EVT-11.Permits: Official permissions from local government for things such as street closures, alcohol service, tents, fireworks or amplified sound.
EVT-11.Request for proposal: A document sent to venues or vendors that describes the event's needs and asks them to bid for the business. It is shortened to RFP.
EVT-11.Banquet event order: A venue's detailed instruction sheet for one function, listing the room setup, timing, menu and equipment. It is shortened to BEO.
EVT-11.Certificate of insurance: Proof from an insurance company that the planner or a vendor holds liability coverage, which venues commonly require.
EVT-11.Site inspection checklist: A form used when visiting a possible venue to record its capacity, condition, access and services for comparison with others.
EVT-11.Staff schedule: A plan showing which staff members and volunteers work where and when during setup, the event and cleanup.
EVT-11.Emergency plan: Written procedures for what to do if something goes wrong, such as severe weather, a fire, a medical emergency or a security threat.
EVT-11.Post-event report: A summary written afterward that compares attendance, spending and feedback with the event's goals and notes lessons for next time.
EVT-11.Marketing plan: A document setting out who the event is aimed at, what messages and channels will be used to reach them and when.
EVT-11.Rooming list: A list sent to a hotel naming each guest in the group's room block with arrival and departure dates and room type.
EVT-11.Event specifications guide: The industry's standard document that gathers every detail and requirement of a large meeting in one place for the venue and suppliers.
EVT-11.Sponsorship prospectus: A document sent to possible sponsors describing the event, its audience and the sponsorship levels and benefits on offer.
EVT-11.Technical rider: An attachment to a performer's contract listing the staging, sound, lighting and hospitality that the organizer must provide.
EVT-11.Load-in schedule: A timetable telling each vendor and exhibitor when and where to deliver, set up and later remove equipment.
EVT-11.Waiver: A form in which a participant accepts the risks of an activity and agrees not to hold the organizer responsible for certain injuries.

EVT-12.Keynote address: The headline speech of a conference, given to the whole audience by a prominent speaker, which sets the theme and tone.
EVT-12.Workshop: A hands-on session in which a small group practices a skill or works through a problem with an instructor.
