EVT-12.Breakout session: One of several smaller sessions held at the same time in different rooms, so attendees choose the topic that interests them most.
EVT-12.Panel discussion: A session in which several experts sit together on stage and discuss a topic, guided by a moderator.
EVT-12.Networking reception: A social gathering, usually with drinks and light food, set up so that attendees can meet one another and make contacts.
EVT-12.General session: A session that all attendees go to together in the main hall, with no other programming at the same time. It is also called a plenary.
EVT-12.Meal function: A breakfast, luncheon, dinner or banquet that is part of the program and often includes a speaker or presentation.
EVT-12.Trade show: The exhibit hall portion of a convention, where companies staff booths to show products and services to attendees.
EVT-12.Awards ceremony: A session, often held with a dinner, that recognizes the achievements of members, competitors or employees.
EVT-12.Seminar: A session in which an expert presents information on one subject to an audience, usually followed by questions.
EVT-12.Coffee break: A short scheduled pause between sessions with drinks and snacks, which gives attendees time to rest, talk and change rooms.
EVT-12.Question-and-answer session: Time set aside, usually at the end of a talk, for the audience to put questions to the speaker.
EVT-12.Roundtable discussion: A small group seated around a table to discuss one topic as equals, with a facilitator in place of a lecturer.
EVT-12.Opening or closing ceremony: The formal start or end of the event, with welcome or farewell remarks from the organizers and sometimes entertainment.
EVT-12.Product demonstration: A session in which a company shows how a product works in front of an audience, often to launch something new.
EVT-12.Poster session: A time when researchers stand beside printed displays of their work and explain it to attendees who walk through.
EVT-12.Fireside chat: An informal on-stage conversation between a moderator and a guest, used in place of a prepared speech.
EVT-12.Pre-conference workshop: A longer, in-depth session held before the main program begins, usually for an extra fee.
EVT-12.Registration: The time and place where arriving attendees check in and collect their name badges and program materials.
EVT-12.Business meeting: The official meeting of an association's members or delegates, where reports are given, votes are taken and officers are elected.
EVT-12.Tours and outings: Organized visits away from the meeting rooms, such as a tour of a local company or a city sightseeing trip.
EVT-12.Entertainment: A concert, party, dance or show put on for attendees, usually in the evening, to make the event more enjoyable.
EVT-12.Lightning talks: A series of very short presentations, each only a few minutes long, given one after another in a single session.
EVT-12.Birds of a feather session: An informal gathering of attendees who share an interest and meet to talk about it without a planned agenda.
EVT-12.Town hall: An open meeting where leaders of the organization answer questions and hear comments from the audience.
EVT-12.Debate: A structured session in which speakers argue opposing sides of a question in front of the audience.
EVT-12.Wellness activity: An optional session such as morning yoga or a fun run that helps attendees stay active and refreshed.
EVT-12.Speed networking: A structured session in which attendees hold a series of short one-on-one meetings, moving to a new partner every few minutes.

EVT-13.Capacity: How many people the space can hold safely and comfortably in the layout the event needs. Too small is unsafe, and too large feels empty.
EVT-13.Cost: The rental fee and all the other charges, which together must fit within the event budget.
EVT-13.Location: Where the venue is. It should be convenient for most of the people expected to attend and suit the image of the event.
EVT-13.Availability: Whether the venue is free on the date and for the hours needed, including time to set up and take down.
EVT-13.Parking: Whether there are enough parking spaces close by for guests who drive, and what guests will be charged to use them.
EVT-13.Atmosphere: The look and feel of the space, such as its style, decor and views, and how well these suit the mood the planner wants.
EVT-13.Catering options: Whether the venue has its own kitchen and caterer, allows outside caterers, and can serve the kind of food the event needs.
EVT-13.Accessibility: Whether guests with disabilities can enter and move around easily, with ramps, elevators and accessible restrooms.
EVT-13.Audiovisual equipment: The sound, lighting, screens, projectors and internet connection the venue provides, and what would have to be rented.
EVT-13.Layout: The shape and arrangement of the rooms, and whether they can be set up the way the program requires, with space for breakouts.
EVT-13.Transportation access: How easily attendees can reach the venue by air, road and public transit, which matters most when guests travel from far away.
EVT-13.Nearby lodging: Whether there are enough hotel rooms at or near the venue for guests who need to stay overnight.
EVT-13.Services and staff: The help the venue provides, such as a coordinator, setup crew, servers and cleaning, and how capable its staff are.
EVT-13.Reputation: What past clients, reviews and references say about the venue's quality and reliability.
EVT-13.Safety and security: How safe the building and its neighborhood are, including fire exits, emergency procedures and security staff.
EVT-13.Rules and restrictions: The venue's policies on matters such as noise, closing time, alcohol, decorations and which outside vendors may be used.
EVT-13.Weather backup: For outdoor events, whether there is a covered or indoor space to move into if the weather turns bad.
EVT-13.Contract terms: The conditions the venue sets, such as the deposit, the payment dates, minimum spending and what happens if the event is canceled.
EVT-13.Fit with the event type: How well the venue suits the purpose, theme and level of formality of the event being planned.
EVT-13.Restrooms: Whether there are enough clean restrooms for the number of guests, close to the event space.
EVT-13.Furniture and equipment included: What comes with the rental, such as tables, chairs, linens, a stage or a dance floor, so the planner knows what must be rented.
EVT-13.Insurance requirements: The liability coverage the venue requires the planner to carry, which adds to the cost of using that site.
EVT-13.Load-in access: How easily vendors can bring in equipment, including loading docks, freight elevators and door sizes.
EVT-13.Acoustics: How sound carries in the room. Echo, or noise from next door, can make speakers hard to hear.
EVT-13.Nearby attractions: Restaurants, shopping and things to do close to the venue, which make an event more appealing to out-of-town attendees.
EVT-13.Ceiling height and sight lines: Whether the room is tall enough for screens and staging, and whether pillars or other obstacles block the view.
EVT-13.Sustainability: The venue's environmental practices, such as recycling, energy saving and reducing food waste, which matter to many clients.
EVT-13.Power supply: Whether the site has enough electrical capacity and outlets for lighting, sound, catering equipment and exhibitors.

SPE-10.Concession stands: Counters around the concourse that sell food and drinks. Concessions are a major source of game-day income for a venue.
SPE-10.Video scoreboard: A giant screen that shows the score, replays, statistics and sponsor messages, so fans in every seat can follow the action.
SPE-10.Luxury suites: Private enclosed rooms with their own seating, catering and restroom, leased mostly to companies that entertain clients there.
SPE-10.Team store: A shop inside the venue that sells jerseys, caps and other licensed merchandise to fans on game day.
SPE-10.Restrooms: Public toilets around the concourse. Newer venues build more of them to cut the lines at halftime and between innings.
SPE-10.Parking: Lots and garages for fans who drive to the game, which also earn income for the team or the venue owner.
SPE-10.Club seating: Premium seats that come with wider chairs, the best views and access to a private indoor lounge with better food and bars.
SPE-10.Wi-Fi: Wireless internet throughout the building, so fans can use the team app, share photos and check other scores from their seats.
SPE-10.Restaurants and bars: Sit-down dining rooms, food halls and bars inside the venue that offer more choice and comfort than a basic stand.
SPE-10.Comfortable seating: Individual seats with backs, armrests, cup holders and more legroom in place of the bench seating of older stadiums.
SPE-10.Roof and climate control: A roof, shade, air conditioning or heating that protects fans from rain, heat and cold. A retractable roof opens in good weather and closes in bad, so games are not rained out.
SPE-10.Sound system: The speakers that carry announcements, music and game sound clearly to every part of the venue.
SPE-10.Fan and kids zones: Areas with games, play equipment and interactive displays that entertain families and children before and during the event.
SPE-10.Accessibility features: Wheelchair seating with companion seats, elevators, ramps and similar features that let fans with disabilities attend.
SPE-10.Mobile app: A phone app that holds digital tickets and lets fans find their seats, order food, watch replays and receive offers.
SPE-10.Tailgating areas: Parking lots and plazas where fans gather to eat and socialize before the game, a tradition at many stadiums.
SPE-10.First aid stations: Staffed medical rooms where fans who are injured or feel ill can get help during an event.
SPE-10.Guest services: A staffed booth where fans can ask questions, report problems, find lost items and get help with tickets or seating.
SPE-10.Team hall of fame: Displays, statues or a museum that honor the team's history and best players, giving fans more to see than the game.
SPE-10.Cashless payment: Stands and shops that take only cards and phone payments, or let fans scan and pay themselves, which shortens the lines.
SPE-10.Security screening: Bag checks and metal detectors at the gates, along with cameras and security staff, that keep the crowd safe.
SPE-10.Ticket office: The windows at the venue where fans buy tickets, collect ones held for them and sort out ticket problems.
SPE-10.Public transit access: A train or bus stop, shuttle service or ride-hailing zone at the venue, so fans can attend without driving.
SPE-10.Party decks: Open group areas with standing room, drink rails or picnic tables, sold to groups or to fans who like to socialize as they watch.
SPE-10.Sensory rooms: Quiet spaces where fans who are overwhelmed by noise and crowds, such as some people with autism, can take a break.
SPE-10.Nursing rooms: Private rooms or pods where parents can feed and care for babies during an event.
SPE-10.Water fountains: Free drinking water and bottle-filling stations, which matter most at hot outdoor games.
SPE-10.ATMs: Cash machines inside the venue. At cashless venues, similar machines turn a fan's cash into a prepaid card.

SPE-11.Team performance: How well the team is playing. Winning teams draw bigger crowds, and attendance usually falls during a losing season.
SPE-11.Ticket prices: What it costs to get in. Higher prices keep some fans away, especially families and casual fans.
SPE-11.Weather: Rain, cold or extreme heat cuts attendance at outdoor events, mostly among fans who planned to buy tickets on the day.
SPE-11.Star players: Famous athletes whom fans will pay to see in person, whether they play for the home team or the visitors.
SPE-11.Opponent: Who the team is playing. A rival, a top-ranked team or a visiting team with a famous player draws a bigger crowd.
SPE-11.Day and time of the game: When the game is played. Weekend and evening games usually outdraw weekday afternoon games, when people are at work or school.
SPE-11.Promotions: Giveaways, theme nights, fireworks and discounts that give fans an extra reason to come to a particular game.
SPE-11.Importance of the game: How much is at stake. Playoff games, title races and season openers attract more fans than ordinary games.
SPE-11.Stadium quality: The comfort, cleanliness and features of the venue. A new or renovated stadium is an attraction in its own right.
SPE-11.Economy: How much money people have to spend. Tickets are a non-essential purchase, so sales suffer when jobs and incomes fall.
SPE-11.Location and access: How easy the venue is to reach by road and public transit, and how far most fans live from it.
SPE-11.Marketing and advertising: How well the team promotes its games through advertising, social media and news coverage.
SPE-11.Competing entertainment: Other ways to spend free time and money, such as other teams, concerts, movies and streaming at home.
SPE-11.Television and streaming: Whether the game can be watched at home. An easy, high-quality broadcast can keep some fans on the couch.
SPE-11.Fan loyalty: How strongly fans feel attached to the team. Loyal fan bases with long traditions keep coming even in bad seasons.
SPE-11.Market size: The number of people living within reach of the venue. A bigger population gives the team more possible ticket buyers.
SPE-11.Parking: How easy and how expensive it is to park near the venue, which adds to the cost and effort of going to a game.
SPE-11.Concession prices: The cost of food and drinks inside. Fans judge the total cost of a night out, not only the ticket.
SPE-11.Game-day entertainment: Everything around the game itself, such as music, halftime shows, contests and the mood of the crowd.
SPE-11.Stadium capacity: The number of seats. Attendance cannot go above it, and a venue that often sells out pushes fans to buy early.
SPE-11.Safety: Whether fans feel safe at the venue and nearby. Fear of crime or unruly crowds keeps families away.
SPE-11.Season ticket base: The number of fans who have already paid for every game, which guarantees a minimum crowd whatever happens.
SPE-11.Holidays and school calendar: Whether children are in school. Family attendance rises in summer and on holidays and falls on school nights.
SPE-11.Novelty of a new team or stadium: A new team or a new building draws curious fans for its first few seasons, a boost often called the honeymoon effect.
SPE-11.Uncertainty of outcome: Fans are more interested when either side could win. Leagues promote competitive balance for this reason.
SPE-11.Roster and coaching changes: Signing a well-known player or hiring a new coach raises fans' hopes and interest before the season starts.
SPE-11.Labor disputes: Strikes and lockouts cancel games, and some fans who are angry about them stay away after play resumes.

SPE-12.Player salaries: What the team pays its athletes under their contracts. For a major professional team this is usually the largest single expense.
SPE-12.Coaching staff salaries: Pay for the head coach, assistant coaches and other coaching specialists who prepare the team.
SPE-12.Travel: Flights, buses, hotels and meals for players and staff going to away games.
SPE-12.Stadium rent: Lease payments to the city, authority or company that owns the venue, for teams that do not own where they play.
SPE-12.Stadium operations: The cost of running the building, including utilities, cleaning, repairs and care of the playing surface.
SPE-12.Equipment and uniforms: Jerseys, protective gear, balls, training equipment and the staff who look after them.
SPE-12.Marketing and advertising: Spending to sell tickets and build the brand, including advertising, promotions and items given away to fans.
SPE-12.Front office salaries: Pay for the business and management staff, such as executives and the ticket sales, marketing, finance and public relations departments.
SPE-12.Game-day staff: Wages for the part-time workers needed at each home game, such as ushers, ticket takers and parking and concession staff.
SPE-12.Medical and training staff: Team doctors, athletic trainers and therapists, along with the treatment and supplies that keep players healthy.
SPE-12.Insurance: Premiums for policies that protect the team, such as liability coverage for the venue and coverage on expensive player contracts.
SPE-12.Security: Guards, police officers and screening equipment that protect fans, players and the building at every event.
SPE-12.Scouting: The cost of finding talent, including scouts' pay and travel to watch amateur, college and rival professional players.
SPE-12.Player development: Funding minor league teams, academies or development squads where young players are trained for the top team.
SPE-12.Training facility: The cost of building, renting and running the practice fields, gym and offices where the team trains.
SPE-12.Taxes: Payroll, property, income and other taxes that the team owes as a business.
SPE-12.Player benefits: Contributions toward players' pensions, health insurance and similar benefits, usually set by the league's labor agreement.
SPE-12.Debt payments: Interest and repayments on money borrowed to buy the team or to build or renovate its stadium.
SPE-12.League fees: Payments each team makes to the league to fund the league office and the services it provides.
SPE-12.Revenue sharing payments: Money that higher-earning teams pay into a pool shared with the other teams in the league, to keep competition balanced.
SPE-12.Signing bonuses: Lump sums promised to players when they sign, along with bonuses paid for reaching performance targets.
SPE-12.Merchandise and concession costs: What the team pays for the jerseys, food and drinks that it sells to fans, known as the cost of goods sold.
SPE-12.Luxury tax: A charge some leagues place on teams whose player payroll goes above a set level, meant to discourage runaway spending.
SPE-12.Technology and analytics: Spending on data analysts, video systems, software and computer networks used by the coaches and the business staff.
SPE-12.Ticketing costs: Fees for the ticketing system, card processing and box office staff needed to sell and deliver tickets.
SPE-12.Legal and professional fees: Payments to lawyers, accountants and consultants for contracts, disputes, audits and advice.
SPE-12.Community relations: The cost of charity programs, youth clinics and player appearances that build goodwill in the team's home area.
SPE-12.Transfer fees: Sums paid to another club for the right to sign a player who is under contract there, a major cost in world soccer.
SPE-12.Broadcast production: The cost of cameras, crews and announcers when a team produces its own game broadcasts and video content.
